what_a_row_is: one thing that first ran, built or was ported, with its level, limits and evidence

rows.title: MSPM0 driver apps ran on a Bluetooth chip
rows.says: 5 of 10 of TI's MSPM0G3507 driver examples built for the CC2340R5 with a 30-line rename header and no app edits. They ran and reached the same waiting point as TI's own CC2340R5 build. Pin states matched except one LED the two sources set differently on purpose.
rows.limits: The other 5 need small app edits. Only what each example shows without a second board or sensor was checked.
rows.why: Code written for a general-purpose chip now runs on a Bluetooth chip, so you can reuse what you already wrote.
rows.image_alt: A CC2340R5 board blinking its LED

rows.title: MSPM0 examples moved to a smaller MSPM0: every one that built and was safe to run, ran
rows.says: Of 361 examples retargeted from the MSPM0G3507 (270) and MSPM0C1104 (91) by changing the device in SysConfig, 153 built for the LP-MSPM0L1306. All 133 that were safe to run (82 and 51) ran on it. None crashed.
rows.limits: Only 62 of the 361 built with no change at all. The rest needed SysConfig lines dropped (a chip limit is suspected, since one configuration was tried), and 13 G3507 ports lost a real setting silently. Each ran without a fault; behavior was checked on a sample.
rows.tag: Unknown (suspected: Chip limit); Tool or docs
rows.why: Programs written for one MSPM0 chip move down to a smaller, cheaper one and keep working.

rows.title: MSPM0 code ran on the new MSPM33
rows.says: 43 of 83 MSPM0G3519 DriverLib examples built for the LP-MSPM33C321A with the app untouched once their SysConfig was carried over. Every GPIO, flash, comparator, timer and polled SPI example among them builds. 40 ran (3 key, flash-protection and boot-configuration examples skipped on purpose). 39 ran with no fault recorded and 1 hit a hard fault.
rows.limits: Of the 40 that did not build, most stop on configuration and naming. SysConfig wants an MSPM33 DMA instance for every DMA channel (8). The crystal pins conflict on the MSPM33 board (7). The app hard-codes DMA where the MSPM33 has DMA0 (3). 6 fail to link. I2C is the MSPM33's different UNICOMM block (4, Chip limit). The hard fault, in timx_timer_mode_periodic_standby, has no cause found.
rows.tag: Tool or docs; Chip limit; Unknown
rows.why: Code from your older MSPM0 projects runs on TI's newer, faster MSPM33 chip.

rows.title: MSPM0 GPIO, UART and timer examples ran on the AM13 motor-control chip
rows.says: All 43 MSPM0G3519 SysConfig files translated to the AM13E230's drivers. 20 built with the app untouched and a 13-line header. All 14 that were safe to run ran with no fault recorded, and the LED examples toggled the pins they should (PA5 to PA8).
rows.limits: Only GPIO, UART, SysTick, timer and SYSCTL examples were tried, and 23 of 43 did not build. The AM13 SDK is pre-release.
rows.why: Your simple MSPM0 programs carry over to a motor-control chip without a rewrite.

rows.title: One app source for the CC23xx and CC27xx
rows.says: Every driver example that both the LP-EM-CC2340R5 and the LP-EM-CC2755P10 ship builds for either board. The app source is byte-identical. Only SysConfig and the linker file differ.
rows.limits: Built, not run across: the CC2755P10 images have not been run from the CC2340R5 source.
rows.why: One program covers two radio chip families, so you write it once.

rows.title: The same TI Drivers app builds on MSPM0 and the CC2340R5
rows.says: All 10 driver examples that the MSPM0 SDK and the F3 SDK both ship build in the other family's project with the app copied byte for byte: 47 shim lines one way, 40 the other, plus a 3 or 4 line SysConfig board overlay for two projects.
rows.limits: Built. Only the first 5 MSPM0 apps have run on a CC2340R5; the other 5 and all 10 CC2340R5 apps on the G3507 have not run. MSPM33 has no TI Drivers layer, so it is not in this table.
rows.why: The same driver code builds for a basic chip and a radio chip, so switching boards costs little.

rows.title: The same C runs from a microcontroller to a Linux processor
rows.says: TI's MSPM0 CMSIS-DSP FFT example ran unchanged on the AM263P's Cortex-R5F and on the SK-TDA4VM's Linux A72 cores. It gave the answer the example expects, checked against the same FFT on a Mac.
rows.limits: One example per target; a small header stands in for CMSIS-core on each.
rows.why: Plain C code you write once runs on a tiny chip and on a Linux processor.

rows.title: Every example on every board, given a verdict before building
rows.says: All 3,411 examples were read in eight TI SDKs for what they need. Every example-to-board pair got a verdict and a named blocker. The cross-builds above test those predictions batch by batch.
rows.limits: A verdict is a prediction until a build or run turns it into a result.
rows.why: Before you spend an evening on an example, a table tells you whether it should work on your board.

rows.title: One app, three software layers, glue counted
rows.says: The same 81-line app built unchanged on DriverLib, TI Drivers and Zephyr. DriverLib needed the least board code (39 lines, 2,352 bytes of flash); Zephyr 68 lines; TI Drivers 49 to 59 plus 136 lines of configuration.
rows.limits: Run on the LP-MSPM0L1306 for DriverLib and Zephyr; the G3507 images are built, not run.
rows.why: You can see how much extra code each software layer costs before you choose one.

rows.title: TI's examples build with one command and no IDE
rows.says: 262 of 270 LP-MSPM0G3507 examples built from a terminal with TI Arm Clang: one make command each, or a shared build script for the 41 whose makefile packaging fails. The same one-command build works for TI examples on the CC2340R5, CC2755P10, CC35X1, L1306 and F2800137 (see the build-from-terminal page).
rows.limits: The other 8 do not build: 4 copies of one bootloader demo have duplicate interrupt vectors, 2 fail to compile under TI Arm Clang 5.1.1, 1 needs a generated file with no build rule, and 1 uses an undeclared timer name.
rows.why: You can build TI's examples from a terminal with one command, no IDE to install first.

rows.title: TI's G3507 examples flashed and run by script, none faulted under the debugger
rows.says: The first 222 LP-MSPM0G3507 examples that built were flashed and run by script; the 40 added by the later build fixes were not run. 213 were flashed and run, and 203 of them ran, none with a fault recorded. 166 were running when checked, and 32 stopped at their own end-of-example breakpoint. 5 stopped at another breakpoint: 2 lacked the second device they talk to, and 3 hit a breakpoint their README does not mention. 9 write the boot configuration and were skipped on purpose.
rows.limits: 10 low-power examples would not flash, or the debugger could not reconnect after them. Started from the reset pin instead, 8 turn their end-of-example breakpoint into a fault. Each ran without a fault under the debugger; what each example did was not checked.
rows.tag: Setup or handling; TI example default
rows.why: A script can flash and run hundreds of TI examples on a real board, so checking a chip does not take days.

rows.title: TI's MSPM0 DriverLib examples build with GCC, and ran on the board
rows.says: All 224 no-RTOS DriverLib examples that ship a GCC makefile for the LP-MSPM0G3507 (136) and LP-MSPM0L1306 (88) built with GCC 12.2 from the Zephyr SDK, with no edits. On the L1306, all 87 that had also run from TI Arm Clang ran from GCC with no fault. 24 showed the same LED or serial behavior as the TI Arm Clang build.
rows.limits: TI names Arm GNU 9-2019-q4, which this comparison does not cover. Code was a median 15% larger with each toolchain's own makefile flags, and C++ examples up to 11.6 times larger from the C++ runtime. Three examples behaved differently only where they read an unconnected pin (comp_hs_dac_vref_external, uart_tx_hw_flow_control, i2c_controller_target_dynamic_switching). The G3507 images are built, not run. The SDK's other GCC projects (other boards, FreeRTOS) are not built.
rows.why: You can use the free GCC compiler on MSPM0 and the examples still run on the board.

rows.title: TI's CC23xx and CC27xx driver examples build with GCC; the radio stacks do not
rows.says: Every F3 SDK example with a GCC makefile for these boards built unchanged with GCC 12.2 from the Zephyr SDK. That is 64 for the LP-EM-CC2340R5 and 80 for the LP-EM-CC2755P10, FreeRTOS and no-RTOS. TI's Bluetooth and Zigbee examples ship no GCC makefile, and their stack libraries ship only for TI Arm Clang (and IAR for Bluetooth).
rows.limits: Built, not run on the boards. The Bluetooth and Zigbee stacks cannot be built with GCC from this SDK as shipped. TI names Arm GNU 12.3.Rel1 for this SDK, which this comparison does not cover; code was 26 to 31% larger at the median, with GCC's makefiles at -O3 and TI Arm Clang's mostly at -Oz.
rows.tag: Setup or handling; Tool or docs
rows.why: The free GCC compiler builds TI's driver examples for the CC23xx and CC27xx radio chips.

rows.title: Which compilers TI's SDKs ship projects for, counted
rows.says: Every example folder in nine SDK folders was scanned (C2000Ware is read twice), counting one per board and kind. TI Arm Clang covers every Arm SDK. GCC covers 1,453 and IAR 1,357 of 1,911 MSPM0 board examples. IAR covers 554 of 643 F3 examples. C2000, AM263P and mmWave have only TI's own compilers.
rows.limits: This is what TI ships, not what builds. GCC is proven on MSPM0 DriverLib. IAR and Keil are not built here.
rows.why: You can see which compilers a TI SDK supports before you pick a tool.

rows.title: ESPHome builds and flashes TI radio boards
rows.says: The cc23xx, cc27xx and cc35xx ESPHome platforms take a YAML file through esphome compile and esphome upload. On the two Zigbee boards, the CC2755P10 joined Home Assistant as a router and switched 32 of 32 times. The CC2340R5 as an end device landed 93 of 100 commands. The CC35X1 joins Wi-Fi, and its ESPHome API answered 20 of 20 commands from a client on the board.
rows.limits: The CC35X1 is not adopted into Home Assistant because the test network keeps clients apart. A second CC2755P10 flash never rejoined until the old device was removed from Home Assistant. On the CC2340R5, 7 of 100 commands timed out, each the first after a quiet spell. Its chip temperature reads about 10 C below the room. A router on that chip linked only with a 2 kB smaller heap, leaving no heap free, in the one configuration tried (a chip limit is suspected).
rows.tag: Setup or handling; Unknown; Unknown (suspected: Chip limit)
rows.why: The popular ESPHome tool can program TI radio boards for your smart home.

rows.title: A TI Zigbee light in Home Assistant with no code on the hub
rows.says: TI's Zigbee light example on the LP-EM-CC2340R5 joined Home Assistant's ZHA on its own and switched in 95 ms. 20 of 20 switches landed.
rows.limits: Not reproduced: the 2026-10-16 repeat did not join Home Assistant in three tries (cause open). Earlier, about two hours after a re-pairing, the same image answered in 3.5 to 7.0 s. One board, one network.
rows.why: A TI Zigbee light shows up in Home Assistant and switches in about a tenth of a second, with no code on the hub.

rows.title: A TI Matter thermostat paired into Apple Home
rows.says: A Matter thermostat built on TI's lighting example for the LP-EM-CC35X1 paired into Apple Home from an iPhone and took a setpoint change from the Home app. TI's unmodified light example paired in 63 s from the Bluetooth connection.
rows.limits: The thermostat's pairing time was not measured. It pairs as an uncertified accessory with a test vendor ID, so Apple Home asks to add it anyway. It was programmed after a full flash erase, because the board keeps the old image's pairing in flash. Apple Home only.
rows.tag: TI example default; Tool or docs
rows.why: A TI board you build pairs into Apple Home like a store-bought smart device.

rows.title: A TI Thread node on the Apple TV's network for an hour
rows.says: A TI Thread node joined the Apple TV's Thread network as a child in under 5 s. Pings from the Mac to the node ran for an hour with 0.44% loss, median 28.5 ms.
rows.limits: Pings the other way, from the node to the Mac, answered 0 of 60, though its pings to its Apple TV parent answered 60 of 60; TI's own CLI image behaves the same. One border router and ping traffic only.
rows.tag: Unknown (suspected: Third-party behavior, the Apple border router not forwarding echo requests)
rows.why: A TI Thread node stays on your home network next to the Apple TV for an hour with almost no lost messages.

rows.title: Zephyr on MSPM0 and CC23xx: one benchmark build, the same score
rows.says: One Zephyr benchmark app ran on the LP-MSPM0G3507 and the LP-EM-CC2340R5 with the same maths. It scored 1.75 CoreMark per MHz on both (Zephyr's GCC, -O2 with loop unrolling). Zephyr also runs on the LP-MSPM0L1306 through an out-of-tree board file.
rows.limits: TI Arm Clang without an operating system scores 2.30 per MHz on the G3507, and plain -O2 under Zephyr 1.63. The L1306 has no upstream Zephyr board; this one is out of tree and the app had to shrink to 4 kB of RAM.
rows.why: The Zephyr operating system gives the same result on two different TI chip families.

rows.title: Zephyr's own samples build for TI's upstream LaunchPad kits
rows.says: Upstream Zephyr 4.4.2 builds 88 of the 93 samples that apply to its four TI LaunchPad boards (hello_world, basic, synchronization, philosophers and drivers). By board: LP-MSPM0G3507 21 of 22, LP-MSPM0G3519 23 of 24, LP-MSPM0L2228 20 of 21, LP-EM-CC2340R5 24 of 26. Hello world takes about 9.4 to 10 kB of flash and 3.8 to 4.1 kB of RAM on each.
rows.limits: Built, not run; the G3519's upstream blinky builds but stopped in a fault handler when run. The mbedtls sample failed on all four because the Zephyr workspace leaves out the mbedtls module. The CC2340R5 flash shell needs 6.9 kB more RAM than the chip has. The L2228 is not on this bench, and the CC2755P10, MSPM33C321A and AM13E230 have no board in Zephyr 4.4.
rows.tag: Setup or handling; Chip limit; Third-party behavior
rows.why: Zephyr's own sample programs build for TI's LaunchPad kits, so you can start from what the community already wrote.

rows.title: An unmodified Arduino graphics library drew on an MSPM0
rows.says: Arduino_GFX's own test example drew on a 3.5 inch screen on the LP-MSPM0G3507 through a 649-line Arduino API layer, with the library's source untouched.
rows.limits: One of two libraries ran; there is no MSPM0 Arduino core from TI to compare against.
rows.why: An Arduino graphics library drew on an MSPM0 chip with a small adapter layer and no changes to the library.

rows.title: FreeRTOS in 4 kB of RAM
rows.says: Eleven FreeRTOS tasks ran on the LP-MSPM0L1306's 4 kB of RAM. The MSPM0 SDK's FreeRTOS makefiles do not build from a terminal as shipped; the build was patched here.
rows.limits: The tasks are small. The count is what fits, not what a real app would use.
rows.why: A small real-time operating system with 11 tasks fits in 4 kB of RAM.

rows.title: A RISC-V hobby AI model reads digits on an MSPM0
rows.says: BitNetMCU, written for WCH's CH32V chips, read all 10 test digits on the LP-MSPM0G3507. At 32 MHz each model took 3.5% to 19% fewer cycles than the author's published CH32V002 figures. At 80 MHz with two flash wait states, like his chip, the most accurate model took 0.5% more. A touch screen version reads a finger-drawn digit.
rows.limits: Cycles were compared against the author's published numbers. No side-by-side run on his chip was made.
rows.why: A hobbyist AI model reads handwritten digits on a tiny MSPM0 chip.
rows.image_alt: The digit-reading demo on the touch screen

rows.title: Another vendor's 5 V microcontroller examples ran on an MSPM0
rows.says: Cmsemicon CMS32F04x pack examples built on the LP-MSPM0L1306 through a glue layer written once (845 lines of C and 409 of headers). 29 main.c files compiled exactly as shipped and 5 had 1 to 15 lines edited. All 34 ran and 21 were checked on the board.
rows.limits: 13 ran without a behavior check, because nothing a probe can see changes; the temperature example prints a wrong value from placeholder trim constants in the glue; of the 19 variants not built, 12 I2C and SPI examples need a second device that was not on the bench and 7 need hardware the L1306 lacks, such as CAN and a segment LCD.
rows.why: Example code written for another vendor's 5 V chip runs on an MSPM0.

rows.title: ST's HAL examples ran on TI's AM13 through TI's STM32 layer
rows.says: Two of ST's HAL examples ran on the LP-AM13E230: GPIO toggle and UART printf, from STM32CubeU0. They went through the STM32G4 compatibility layer TI ships in the AM13 SDK, with a few lines added and none changed.
rows.limits: TI's layer has 65 of the 93 functions its headers declare and no timers, ADC or I2C, so ST's timer examples do not compile.
rows.why: Code written for ST's HAL runs on a TI motor-control chip through a layer that translates it.

rows.title: A TI Bluetooth chip answers Nordic's LED Button and UART services
rows.says: The LP-EM-CC2340R5 advertises Nordic's LED Button Service and UART Service from one image. Those are the services Nordic's nRF Blinky and nRF Toolbox phone apps use. A Bluetooth client on a Mac wrote the LED characteristic (24.3 ms) and got 60 of 60 UART lines echoed back.
rows.limits: Nordic's phone apps and the board's button were not used. They wait on a person with a phone at the bench. Not certified.
rows.why: A TI Bluetooth chip works with apps made for Nordic's LED, button and serial services.
rows.image_alt: A Bluetooth scanner showing the board

rows.title: A TI sub-1 GHz radio sent every one of its modes, OFDM included, from an MSPM0
rows.says: An LP-MSPM0G5187 drove a CC1407P radio through TI's host driver and sent all 23 of TI's radio settings. That includes every OFDM mode, from 0.69 kbps to about 2.2 Mbps. 345 of 345 packets went out, each rate within 3.4% of TI's figure where TI gives one.
rows.limits: Transmit only for OFDM: no OFDM receiver was on the bench, so no OFDM packet was heard. Only the two Wi-SUN FSK modes were received (260 of 260 each). One mode, SUN O-QPSK, failed the checksum at the receiver.
rows.tag: Setup or handling; Unknown (suspected: packet format)
rows.why: One MSPM0 chip drives a TI sub-1 GHz radio through every one of its modes.

rows.title: One command takes an LP-MSPM0L1306 to a pattern you chose, checked on the board
rows.says: `./start.sh mspm0l1306 blink --probe <serial>` backed up the board, built TI's blink example with the asked LED pattern, flashed it and timed the LED pin through the debugger: 13 to 14 s with the tools installed.
rows.limits: One board model, one Intel Mac with the tools already installed. The check times the LED pin through the debugger; the LED itself was not inspected. Apple Silicon and Linux built images that blinked correctly, but flashing from them is untested; Windows is untested.
rows.why: One command puts a pattern on an LP-MSPM0L1306 and checks it worked, in about 13 seconds.

rows.title: A Hall-sensor brushless motor spun from the LP-AM13E230 through TI's DRV8376EVM, no motor BoosterPack
rows.says: The DRV8376EVM plugs onto the LaunchPad kit's headers as it is. A 350-line six-step program learns the Hall table by itself (holding the rotor on the six phase axes, then scoring twelve candidate tables by how far the rotor travels) and ran an Anaheim BLY171S-24V-4000 forward at 924, 2,312 and 3,632 rpm at 20, 40 and 60 percent duty on a 12.4 V bus (891, 2,091 and 3,442 rpm in reverse), with a brake and fault clear, all from a serial terminal.
rows.limits: Open loop in duty, unloaded, one motor. The EVM's phase-voltage read-back was not usable for finding the PWM mode; the mode is forced to 6x. Speed is from Hall edge timing, not a tachometer. No current loop.
rows.why: A brushless motor spins from an LP-AM13E230 through TI's driver board, with no extra motor BoosterPack.
rows.image_alt: The AM13 board wired to the motor driver board

rows.title: DRV8376 commissioning restored bounded motor rotation
rows.says: After TI startup calibration, a measured current-limit reference and a new Hall table enabled two-second trapezoidal trials with 133 and 279 consecutive forward Hall sectors and no driver fault.
rows.limits: The diagnostic six-step controller ran. Closed-loop TI FOC, calibrated current gain, speed regulation and load tests remain unverified.
rows.why: A motor that had stopped turning runs again, so you know the setup steps work.
rows.image_alt: The AM13 board wired to the motor driver board

rows.title: Equipment telemetry from a CC2340R5 tag to a CC35X1 hub and a phone
rows.says: A CC2340R5 tag advertised a simulated machine's counters on legacy and extended sets at once; a CC35X1 hub with its own access point and the house Wi-Fi logged 283 of 283 events, median 1.4 s, totals identical to the equipment's, and served them to a phone app; the tag's run-event classifier was 95.9% right on live run events.
rows.limits: The equipment was simulated over USB, or the tag's own buttons stood in for it (9 run events, 2 jams on 2026-10-17); the AM13E230 motor telemetry is built, not run; a phone has not been confirmed on the hub's own access point; data on the air is not encrypted.
rows.why: A small tag on a piece of equipment sends readings over Bluetooth to a hub and a phone, with none lost.

rows.title: TI's own Hall FOC runs closed-loop speed control on the LP-AM13E230 and DRV8376EVM
rows.says: TI's AM13 Hall-sensored FOC solution, ported to the DRV8376EVM, calibrated its Hall table, aligned the BLY171S, ramped open loop to 30 Hz, closed the loop and brought the motor down to its 10 Hz reference: 129 rpm against 150 commanded over the last second, no fault, to the 12 s cap.
rows.limits: One bounded 12 s run, unloaded, one motor, 12.4 V. The DRV8376 cycle-by-cycle current limit was off; with it on, its nFAULT report tripped the PWM at the handover. Four SDK faults are patched in the port, one of them (a Hall speed filter that diverges below about 38 kHz PWM) specific to running at 20 kHz. Speed was still settling and there was no load test. Later runs through the motor link do not hold this result: runs at 20 Hz fault more often than not, and a reversal and a speed step both fail.
rows.tag: Setup or handling; TI example default
rows.why: TI's own motor firmware holds a set speed on a real motor.
rows.image_alt: The AM13 board wired to the motor driver board

rows.title: An AI assistant reads TI's AM13 motor firmware live, through TI's own MotorVision protocol
rows.says: The host client speaks the MotorVision UART protocol from the AM13E2x SDK source, with no vendor GUI: TI's Hall FOC firmware streamed at 9.2 Mbaud over the LaunchPad kit's USB serial port to a Mac, and an MCP server let Claude read the motor state, decoded faults, bus voltage and currents.
rows.limits: Read-only and idle: the motor did not run under this link. TI's AM13 GUI was not public, so nothing was compared against it. Two SDK file problems are worked around in the client: the variable map disagrees with the firmware table, and the receiver never resynchronises.
rows.why: An AI assistant can read live values from a running motor, so you can ask it what the motor is doing.
rows.image_alt: The motor console beside the phone view

rows.title: A MotorVision client ran TI's Hall FOC through speed, current, step and reversal tests on the LP-AM13E230 and DRV8376EVM
rows.says: motorlink started, held and stopped the motor itself under the board's guard (43 starts, 6.3 s to one turn). With TI's default gains the speed estimate is spiky (isolated reads of hundreds of Hz) and the current amplitude wanders 130 to 300 percent over a 5 s window at 10, 20 and 30 Hz electrical. Only 3 of 14 runs at 20 Hz reached the 20 s cap, the rest ended in TI's hardware over-current fault; 7 of 7 reversals from +20 to -20 Hz faulted within 0.3 to 2 s; a 20 to 30 Hz step rose in 0.5 to 1.5 s with 23 to 137 percent overshoot and never settled.
rows.limits: Unloaded, one motor, 12.4 V, TI's default gains (not tuned), host polling at 188 to 375 samples a second per variable, the step speed taken from Hall edge counts, no current or power instruments. Why the faults happen is not isolated. Efficiency, torque, noise, temperature, stall, sensorless and current-loop bandwidth did not run, each for a named missing instrument or build.
rows.tag: Setup or handling; TI example default
rows.why: A scripted test run puts a real motor through speed, current, step and reversal checks, and the report says which passed.
rows.image_alt: The motor console during a test run

rows.title: A pin, a timer, PWM and a bus set from the browser, no code
rows.says: The Digital Lab's controls card is a short list of settings. A plus adds one I/O (a pin, a timer toggle, a PWM at a frequency and duty, a bus scan, a register read), each row shows the line of C it stands for, a minus removes it, and the board drawing lights the chosen pin with its setup. A BoosterPack picked from a list brings its own rows (predicted: none is plugged onto this board). One 4 kB program on the LP-MSPM0L1306 applies one 84-byte table the page writes to the last flash sector. Run in Chrome on a Mac: PA26 at 200 and 300 ms timed 200 to 203 and 294 to 299 ms, PA13 at 100 and 400 ms, a pin driven high and low and read back, six PWM settings from 100 Hz to 20 kHz whose timer registers and counter matched, and a bus scan that found nothing; then the board's saved copy went back, read back identical.
rows.limits: One board (the L1306; the program is built from TI's I2C example for that kit). One pin and four register reads at a time. The page times the pin's output register, not the LED. A PWM pad is judged through its timer (registers and counter), not on the pad: the GPIO input register does not follow a timer-driven pad. No register read has been answered by a part, and the BoosterPack rows are predicted. A bus scan says who acknowledged, not what the part is. Times under 5 ms and over 10 s are clamped.
rows.why: You set a pin, a timer, PWM or a bus from the browser with no code to write.

rows.title: Post-quantum key exchange and signatures run on the MSPM33C321A with code written for another chip
rows.says: The portable ML-KEM-768 and ML-DSA-44 code that first ran on the CC1354P10 runs unchanged on the LP-MSPM33C321A at 160 MHz and passes every NIST known-answer test: ML-KEM-768 key pair, encapsulate and decapsulate in 8.1, 9.2 and 11.3 ms, ML-DSA-44 key pair 19 ms, verify 19 ms, sign 39 ms for one message. Only the board glue (cycle counter, stack painting) is new.
rows.limits: Cycle counts are 30 percent above the CC1354P10's with the same compiler (2 flash wait states here, none there). No TRNG or serial exchange with a Mac was run here. ML-DSA signing needs 51 kB of stack.
rows.why: Encryption designed to resist future quantum computers runs on the MSPM33 with code written for another chip.

rows.number: 6 of 6 post-quantum steps pass on a Cortex-M0+
rows.title: Post-quantum key exchange and signatures run on the MSPM0G3519, a Cortex-M0+ with no cycle counter, with code written for another chip
rows.says: The portable ML-KEM-768 and ML-DSA-44 code from the CC1354P10 runs unchanged on the LP-MSPM0G3519 at 80 MHz and passes every NIST known-answer test: ML-KEM-768 key pair, encapsulate and decapsulate in 24.6, 29.1 and 35.6 ms, ML-DSA-44 key pair 82 ms, verify 95 ms, sign 317 ms for one message. Only the board glue is new: SysTick for the cycle count (the M0+ has no DWT), a RAM log the debugger reads, and a 60 kB stack in the second SRAM bank.
rows.limits: Cycle counts are about 2 times the CC1354P10's for ML-KEM and 2.8 to 3.4 times for ML-DSA, within 9 percent of TI's own published library figures. No TRNG or serial exchange with a Mac was run here. ML-DSA-44 signing needs 51.8 kB of stack, so it does not fit parts with 32 kB of RAM.
rows.why: Quantum-resistant encryption runs on a small Cortex-M0+ chip that has no cycle counter.

rows.title: The CC2755P10 closes a Q15 digital-power loop up to 331 kHz, 3.4 times the CC2340R5, from the same C code
rows.says: The PID program written for the CC2340R5 ran on the LP-EM-CC2755P10 after three changes: both clocks from the board table (CPU 96 MHz, timer and ADC 48 MHz), the ADC pin, and a longer timer-ratio count. The PWM zero event triggers the ADC, the result interrupt runs the PID and writes the duty. Trigger to duty write is 282 cycles in Q15 (worst 284) and 294 in float (worst 342) at 100 kHz, against 410 and 2,016 on the CC2340R5. The highest rate with no missed interrupt, late duty write or ADC overflow is 331 kHz in Q15 and 318 kHz in float at -O2 (338 and 329 at -O3), the same on three runs to the timer count, with 23.5 and 26.5 percent of a 100 kHz period spent in the interrupt.
rows.limits: One board, input pin floating (nothing wired), so the ADC sample is noise and the duty is not a real converter's. The rates are timer-count steps of 0.2 to 0.4 percent. The interrupt entry is 128 CPU cycles after the PWM zero, mostly the ADC conversion, so the highest rate is set by latency and handler together.
rows.why: The same digital-power loop code runs 3.4 times faster on this chip than on the CC2340R5, with the FPU making float nearly as quick as Q15.

rows.title: Post-quantum code ran unchanged on the CC2755P10, and its HSM does P-256 in 24 ms
rows.says: The ML-KEM-768 and ML-DSA-44 code that first ran on the CC1354P10 runs on the LP-EM-CC2755P10 at 96 MHz and passes every NIST known-answer test: ML-KEM-768 key pair, encapsulate and decapsulate in 10.0, 11.6 and 14.1 ms; ML-DSA-44 key pair 23.9 ms, sign 49.7 ms (one message), verify 24.3 ms. Cycle counts are 3 percent below the CC1354P10's. TI's driver for the chip's HSM signs P-256 in 24 ms against 81 ms for the best software build.
rows.limits: The HSM signature has no known-answer vector (TI's example vector does not verify on its own); it is checked by the HSM's own verify and a flipped-bit rejection. ML-DSA signing needs 51 kB of stack. No TRNG or Mac exchange was run here.
rows.why: Quantum-resistant encryption code runs unchanged on a radio chip, and its security engine does P-256 in 24 ms.

rows.title: Post-quantum key exchange runs on the MSPM0G5187, a Cortex-M0+ with 32 kB of RAM
rows.says: The portable ML-KEM-768 code from the CC1354P10 runs on the LP-MSPM0G5187 at 80 MHz and passes every NIST known-answer test: key pair, encapsulate and decapsulate in 24.9, 29.8 and 36.4 ms at -Os, using 14 to 18 kB of stack. The same board glue as the G3519 port, with the unused buffers dropped at link and a 3 kB RAM log.
rows.limits: ML-DSA-44 signatures do not fit: they need 31 to 52 kB of stack. -O3 does not fit either (encapsulation needs 20.5 kB). No TRNG or serial exchange with a Mac was run here.
rows.why: Quantum-resistant key exchange fits in 32 kB of RAM on a low-cost chip.

rows.title: Sensorless FOC on the AM13 with no Halls: TI's FAST, run in TI's own Hall firmware, drives from align to 40 Hz
rows.says: TI's AM13 Hall FOC builds its FAST and ESMO observers but never runs them. The port runs one beside the Halls. A current-minimum sweep found TI's calibrated Hall table 49 degrees off the rotor; FAST read the angle to about 3 degrees with no help. In Hall-free mode TI's align and open-loop start hand straight to FAST, the Halls logged only as a referee: two of two 20 s runs held 40.0 Hz with no fault at 0.063 A, against 0.13 A on TI's Halls. ESMO with a fixed 31 degree trim did the same. Earlier the Halls trained the observer and handed over at 30 Hz.
rows.limits: Unloaded, one motor, 12.4 V, one speed (40 Hz); no loaded start, low speed, reversal or step on the observer. The Halls stay wired as a referee; the firmware does not use them in Hall-free mode. ESMO's trim came from this motor's sweep. The sweep's answer rests on a 1/cos current fit over six points (45 to 52.5 degrees band).
rows.why: A motor runs without Hall sensors at about half the current, so a design can drop the sensors and their wires.

rows.title: Upstream OpenOCD flashes the LP-EM-CC2340R5 with a new cc23xx driver: blink programmed, verified and reset in 0.37 s, no CCStudio (TI's own OpenOCD fork has its own driver; this one is for upstream master)
rows.says: Upstream OpenOCD had drivers for the older CC13x0 and CC26xx and nothing for CC23xx or CC27xx; TI's own OpenOCD fork (github.com/TexasInstruments/ti-openocd, branch ti-release, head cb22a31e of 2026-07-02, GPL-2.0-or-later) already carries cc23xx, cc27xx, mspm33 and am13e230x flash drivers and board files, shipped as Mac builds with TI's VS Code debug extension; upstream OpenOCD master has none of the CC23xx and CC27xx parts. This is an upstream-master driver; TI's fork has its own. A new flash driver resets the chip through SACI, halts it in the boot ROM and calls the ROM's own sector erase and program routines. Identity and a 512 kB dump matched DSLite byte for byte, one sector erased and wrote in 10 and 34 ms, TI's blink programmed and verified in 0.37 s with the LED pin toggling, and the 511 kB tag image went back in 10.5 s and read back identical.
rows.limits: One chip, one board, one day. The CC2755P10 path builds and has not run. The driver never writes CCFG or SCFG, so an SDK hex that carries a CCFG user record fails verify; flash the main image alone. OpenOCD's exit needed a dormant command before DSLite would connect again. Not upstreamed.
rows.why: You can flash a CC2340R5 in under half a second with a free 10 MB tool and no CCStudio.

rows.title: A brushless motor spins on the MSPM33 LaunchPad through the DRV8376 driver board
rows.says: A six-step Hall program, written for the board from scratch since the MSPM33 SDK ships no motor library, found the forward commutation table by trial and turned the BLY171S at about 160 rpm for 3.3 s at a 6 percent on time from a 20 V pack, peak phase current 0.40 A, with no trip.
rows.limits: Unloaded, one run. Software PWM at 20 kHz, not a timer. The driver's own cycle-by-cycle current limit was off: this LaunchPad has no DAC on the pin that feeds it.
rows.why: A brushless motor spins on the new MSPM33 LaunchPad through TI's driver board.

rows.title: Hall FOC from the portable motor core runs on the MSPM33 LaunchPad
rows.says: A float Hall FOC, with the control math from the board-independent motor core, measured its own Hall table by sweeping the field angle, started the BLY171S and held the d-axis current at zero and the q-axis current on its reference until the 1.5 V cap: 685 rpm, 63 mA of torque current, which is the motor's measured friction. The voltage balance from the measured resistance, back-EMF and dead band predicts 1.51 V against 1.495 V applied.
rows.limits: Unloaded, current loop only (no speed loop), one run. The control loop takes 32 to 35 percent of the CPU at 160 MHz with library trig and a busy wait. The driver's own current limit is off on this LaunchPad.
rows.why: A smooth, efficient motor drive method runs on the MSPM33 from motor code written to be portable.

rows.title: The Sharp128 memory screen runs from an LP-MSPM0C1104 with no frame buffer
rows.says: The BOOSTXL-SHARP128 panel is drawn line by line from a 4.9 kB program that uses 609 bytes of RAM, 352 of them stack. A full redraw takes 41.1 ms in 16-row bands and 153.7 ms in 1-row bands at a 1 MHz clock. The counter on the panel was seen counting.
rows.limits: One board. The microSD player is built and simulated on the Mac but has not read a real card. Start-up time to first picture is not measured.
rows.why: A memory screen runs from the smallest MSPM0 with only 609 bytes of RAM.

rows.title: The Educational BoosterPack MKII core runs on an LP-MSPM0L1306
rows.says: A portable core for the BoosterPack screen, stick, buttons, buzzer, accelerometer, microphone and light sensor ran its hello example on the LP-MSPM0L1306: light sensor IDs read, joystick Y, accelerometer X and Y and the microphone read plausible values.
rows.limits: Joystick X reads about 3 counts, probably the light-sensor amplifier through jumper J4 (left in place). The screen path does not fit this LaunchPad without wires: three of its pins are the debug pins. LED, buzzer and press were not observed.
rows.why: A popular training BoosterPack works with a low-cost LP-MSPM0L1306, with four of its six sensors read.

rows.title: Snake is drawn on the Educational BoosterPack screen from the LP-MSPM33C321A
rows.says: The Educational BoosterPack screen path (DMA blit) and an Arduboy2-compatible layer drew the open-source Snake game on the screen; the main flash was read twice and checked identical before the flash.
rows.limits: Seen on the bench camera only: stick, frame rate and the sound are not judged. The expected frame rate is 40 to 50 a second.
rows.why: The classic Snake game plays on the BoosterPack screen from the MSPM33 LaunchPad.

rows.title: The Educational BoosterPack core builds for four more LaunchPad kits
rows.says: The same core builds for the LP-MSPM33C321A, LP-MSPM0G3519, LP-MSPM0G3507 and LP-MSPM0G5187 at 13.8 to 16.5 kB of flash and 0.9 to 1.2 kB of RAM, with pin maps generated from one pins.json per board and clashes the matrix lacked recorded.
rows.limits: Built only; the screen path ran on one board (see Snake).
rows.why: The same BoosterPack code builds for four more LaunchPad kits, so one project can follow you across boards.

rows.title: The BOOSTXL-AUDIO pack plays a tone and a tune from an LP-AM13E230
rows.says: A plain GPIO driver sends 16-bit frames to the DAC8311 and the pack microphone reads 1000.0 Hz with 99.9 percent of the energy within 50 Hz. A four-voice tune played and the dominant frequency read 1046.5 Hz. Both were also heard by ear.
rows.limits: Bit-banged lines, DAC on SPI only, volume 4 for an unclipped capture. Two 8-bit transfers instead of one 16-bit frame give silence in every amplifier state. The pack cannot be driven on the LP-MSPM0G5187 without wires.
rows.why: An audio BoosterPack plays a clean 1000 Hz tone and a tune from a motor-control chip.

rows.title: The Sensors MKII pack reads three sensors from an LP-MSPM0G5187
rows.says: With the CC1407 pack also stacked, the HDC2080 read 22.0 C and 44.7 percent RH, the OPT3001 about 4000 lux and the DRV5055 1.638 V. A 100 Hz stream loop kept 100.000 Hz for 62.4 s with no gap over 15 ms.
rows.limits: TMP117 and BMI160 never answered and no cause is found. The 100 Hz run used a stand-in for the motion data. BMM150 and the LEDs were not run.
rows.why: A sensor BoosterPack reads three of its sensors from an LP-MSPM0G5187.
rows.image_alt: The Sensors BoosterPack on an LP-MSPM0G5187

rows.title: Zephyr shields for three BoosterPacks build on MSPM0 LaunchPad kits
rows.says: The Educational screen, the Sharp128 memory display and the Audio DAC build as Zephyr shields on the LP-MSPM0G3519 and LP-MSPM0G3507 with Zephyr main, which has an MSPM0 SPI driver since 2026-04-21 (release 4.4.2 has none).
rows.limits: Built only; nothing was flashed. The MSPM33 board file in Zephyr main has no SPI node, so no shield builds there. Backlight and chip-select polarity are unconfirmed.
rows.why: Zephyr descriptions for three BoosterPacks build on MSPM0 LaunchPad kits, so those packs plug into Zephyr projects.

rows.title: A fixed-weight FIR filter runs on the MSPM0G5187 NPU
rows.says: A 64-tap FIR as a fixed-weight convolution compiled by NNC 2.1.2 runs 4 x 256 outputs in 0.566 ms, 29.7 times faster than the same graph on the CPU and 5.8 times faster than one hand-written C channel. The output equals the integer reference byte for byte. A filter bank (0.967 ms), a strided FIR, a comparator and a DFT also ran.
rows.limits: 8-bit end to end, about 35 dB. Output channels come in multiples of 4. The DFT reached only 0.26 multiply-adds per cycle, 4.3 times the CPU.
rows.why: The chip's AI hardware runs a signal filter about 30 times faster than its CPU.

rows.title: A DNS ad blocker runs on the LP-EM-CC35X1
rows.says: The board answers DNS on UDP port 53. 71,492 blocked names, held as a 357 kB hash table in flash, get 0.0.0.0 in a median of 6 ms; other names are forwarded and relayed in a median of 70 ms. Transaction IDs come from the chip hardware random generator.
rows.limits: IPv4 and UDP only, exact-name match. The 304,000-name ceiling is link arithmetic, not a loaded run.
rows.why: A tiny TI board can block ad domains for the whole network and answer in 6 ms.

rows.title: MicroPython boots on an LP-MSPM0G3519
rows.says: The full MicroPython 1.29.0 build prints its banner on the backchannel UART at 115200 baud, reports 80 MHz and 121,824 bytes of heap free, and does floating-point arithmetic. No MSPM0 port was found upstream, so this is a new port.
rows.limits: Raw binary flash only (the ELF stopped at 91 percent). A pin toggle ran without error but the LED could not be judged. No speed number. The LP-MSPM0G3507 has a minimal build that is not flashed.
rows.why: You can type Python at a prompt on an MSPM0G3519, with no compiler in the loop.

rows.title: 2048 and Minesweeper run on an LP-MSPM0G3519 with a touch screen
rows.says: Both games draw through two display calls and read one touch call. A 2048 swipe redraws in 32.6 ms at a 40 MHz SPI clock and a one-cell Minesweeper tap in 1.09 ms; 215 host checks pass. The scripted boot run drives the same code path a finger uses.
rows.limits: The 40 MHz clock is above the panel rating of about 15 MHz. No finger touched the board in the recorded runs (the touch counter read 0 after 222 polls), so touch-to-pixel delay and Minesweeper by finger are not measured.
rows.why: 2048 and Minesweeper play on a touch screen driven by a small MSPM0 chip.

rows.title: Three Arduboy games build unchanged on four MSPM0 and MSPM33 LaunchPad kits
rows.says: An Arduboy2-compatible layer of about 700 lines runs Snake, TileWorld and Crate Confusion on a Mac host with scripted input and links for four boards at 5.5 to 9.6 kB of flash. Snake then drew on a board screen.
rows.limits: No Arduboy FX, rounded shapes or triangles; EEPROM lives in RAM.
rows.why: Three small Arduboy games build unchanged for four TI LaunchPad kits.

rows.title: A Game Boy emulator runs a game on the Mac and links for two LaunchPad kits
rows.says: Peanut-GB 1.3.0 passes the dmg-acid2 picture and plays Tobu Tobu Girl on the host at about 4,180 frames per second (CPU time). It links for the LP-MSPM0G3519 and LP-MSPM33C321A with a 256 kB ROM in flash.
rows.limits: Host only, no sound; the LP-MSPM0G3507 and LP-MSPM0G5187 cannot hold the ROM. Two out-of-bounds bugs were patched in the build copy.
rows.why: A Game Boy emulator plays a game on the Mac and builds for two LaunchPad kits, a first step toward playing on them.

rows.title: Doom runs on the LP-EM-CC35X1
rows.says: The engine reads the unchanged shareware data file in place from flash (SHA-1 matches), draws the same first 400 frames as the Mac build (checksum 8ceeaad8) and runs the first demo at 50 to 66 frames per second with no screen output.
rows.limits: All three demos stop on zone memory: demo 1 at frame 2030 of 5,025, demo 2 at frame 52, demo 3 at frame 425 (its frames differ from the Mac after frame 100, cause not found). No screen or keys; the demo select byte never reached the firmware.

rows.title: Doom does not fit the LP-MSPM0G3519, LP-MSPM0G3507 or LP-MSPM33C321A
rows.says: Static data alone stops the two MSPM0 boards, and the LP-MSPM33C321A links only with an 80 kB zone. The three shareware demos run to the end in a Cortex-M33 emulator with frame checksums equal to the Mac.
rows.limits: Emulator, not the chip. The CC35X1 is the smallest TI chip found that runs it.

rows.title: Three Arduboy games and a Game Boy emulator run on the Educational BoosterPack screen from an LP-MSPM33C321A
rows.says: Snake, TileWorld and Crate Confusion run at 30.6 to 32.9 frames per second (30 to 33 ms a frame, 25.6 ms of it the screen). One 128 by 128 frame takes 19.5 ms by DMA at 16 MHz against 55.3 ms polled. The Game Boy emulator started at about 6.7 frames per second and now plays at the console's own speed (see the Game Boy milestone).
rows.limits: One board. Sound is a buzzer toggle; the stick and buttons were judged only for Snake's scripted press. The first Game Boy image ran at 8 to 13 percent of real speed with no sound.
rows.why: Small games and a Game Boy emulator play on the BoosterPack screen at 31 to 33 frames a second.

rows.title: A guitar tuner, spectrum bars, a DTMF decoder and a noise gate with echo build for two LaunchPad kits
rows.says: Portable integer C for the Audio BoosterPack: a pitch tracker within 0.22 cents on clean tones from 82 to 200 Hz (9.5 cents worst case on guitar-like tones near 1 kHz), 16 spectrum bars within 1.3 pixels, and a DTMF decoder that holds to about 1 dB of noise. Builds for the LP-AM13E230 (29.6 kB of flash) and the LP-MSPM33C321A (23.1 kB).
rows.limits: Checked on the Mac against double-precision references; not run on a board and no cycle counts.
rows.why: A guitar tuner, spectrum bars, a DTMF decoder and a noise gate build for two LaunchPad kits.

rows.title: MicroPython drives a touch screen on an LP-MSPM0G3519
rows.says: Hardware machine.SPI fills 320 by 480 pixels in 147 ms at 20 MHz and two Python files draw fills, rectangles and text; the touch chip answers and reads in 1.43 ms. Two port bugs were found on the board and fixed.
rows.limits: SPI1 only, 20 MHz maximum on this panel, no file system so the files are re-sent after a reset. Finger tracking is not checked by a person.
rows.why: Python code reads and draws on a touch screen from a small MSPM0 chip.

rows.title: A small language model writes a story on an LP-MSPM33C321A
rows.says: TinyStories 260K (llama2.c, int8) runs 128 tokens from flash at 160 MHz in 7.47 million cycles per token. All 128 token ids equal a Cortex-M33 emulator run; the first 39 equal the Mac build.
rows.limits: One model of 260,000 parameters and 128 steps; the sentences are short and repetitive. After token 39 the Mac and the chip differ in library math, not in the port.
rows.why: A small language model writes a short story on a microcontroller, at about 21 words a second.

rows.title: A WebAssembly interpreter builds for three LaunchPad kits
rows.says: wasm3 v0.9.0 is 56.7 kB of flash on the Cortex-M0+ LP-MSPM0G3519 and 78.1 kB on the Cortex-M33 LP-MSPM33C321A; a tiny configuration fits the 32 kB RAM of the LP-MSPM0G3507 in 11.1 kB. A 346-byte module gives the C answers in emulators of both cores.
rows.limits: Emulator and Mac only, nothing flashed. Two safety defects found in the interpreter (call_ref stack, memory.grow) are patched in a build copy; the upstream reports are not filed.
rows.why: A WebAssembly interpreter builds for three LaunchPad kits, so the same compiled module could run on any of them.

rows.title: Rust blinks an LED and prints over serial on an LP-MSPM0L1306
rows.says: A Rust blinky is 2,636 bytes of flash and 112 bytes of RAM; a serial hello is 3,744 bytes. From nothing to a blinking LED took about 2.7 minutes on a Mac, and the LED pin check passed.
rows.limits: Community hardware layer (embassy-mspm0), not supported by TI. Only GPIO, the timer driver and the blocking UART were run.
rows.why: Rust code blinks an LED and prints over serial on a basic MSPM0, in 2.6 kB.

rows.title: The rp2040-doom design fits the 256 kB of an LP-MSPM33C321A in an emulator
rows.says: Linked into the chip's real RAM map, the engine leaves 58.0 kB for the zone; with a 30 kB zone it needs 228 kB. All three shareware demos play to the end in a Cortex-M33 emulator with 28.9 kB of zone in use.
rows.limits: This milestone is the emulator step; the chip ran it afterwards (see the board milestone). The data file is 1.72 MB, more than the 1 MB of flash, so the chip reads it from the on-board QSPI flash through a page cache.

rows.title: Doom plays all three demos to the end on the LP-EM-CC35X1
rows.says: The rp2040-doom design reads the converted game data in place from flash and plays three shareware demos at 39.2 frames per second with the render files at -O2 (36.7 at -Os) and a 40 kB zone (28.9 kB used); hot data in the 1-cycle TCM and a RAM cache for level data raised it from 22.5. The frame chain after demo 3, fc7b6c2d, equals the emulator run at both optimisation levels.
rows.limits: No panel, keys or sound. The 22.5 was a placement problem: a load costs 6.2 cycles in DRAM, 1.06 in TCM and 44 from flash. The data cache covers PSRAM only. The reference is the emulator, not a Mac build. An earlier reference, e9db8f1d, came from an engine that read an uninitialized stack array; the fix is in the build copy.

rows.title: A Game Boy game plays at full console speed on the Educational BoosterPack screen
rows.says: Peanut-GB runs Tobu Tobu Girl on the LP-MSPM33C321A at 160 MHz with a table scaler, DMA rows and one frame in two drawn: 0 of 8,167 emulated frames finished late at the console's 59.7 frames per second. The first image ran at 8 to 13 percent of that.
rows.limits: No sound. The screen shows every second frame (about 30 a second). The stick and buttons were not judged by a person. The unpaced top speed was not read on the board.
rows.why: A Game Boy game plays at full console speed on a BoosterPack screen, with no late frames.

rows.title: A language model writes its story live on a BoosterPack screen
rows.says: TinyStories 260K draws every token on the Educational BoosterPack screen of an LP-MSPM33C321A as it is produced, with word wrap and scrolling: 19.1 tokens per second with the display on against 21.1 with the drawing time taken out. A new story starts every 30 s; 9 finished in the first 4 minutes.
rows.limits: The S2 button that starts a new story was not pressed. Drawing costs about 10 percent of the speed. One model of 260,000 parameters.
rows.why: A language model shows its story on a BoosterPack screen as it writes it.

rows.title: A WebAssembly interpreter runs on the LP-MSPM0G3519
rows.says: wasm3 v0.9.0 runs a 346-byte module on the Cortex-M0+ board at 80 MHz and prints PASS: fib(20) takes 167.0 ms against 3.84 ms for the same C (43.5 times) and a 20,000-pass loop 173.9 ms against 6.01 ms (28.9 times). After a per-pass heap leak was fixed, 14 passes in 60 s kept the heap flat at 6.9 kB of 16 kB.
rows.limits: One board. The G3507 and M33 images are not flashed. The emulator estimate (37 and 19 times) was low.
rows.why: A WebAssembly interpreter runs on the MSPM0G3519, and a program that runs through it works on the board.

rows.title: The rp2040-doom design plays all three demos on an LP-MSPM33C321A from its QSPI flash
rows.says: The 16 MB QSPI flash was read twice with identical results, the 1,758 kB Doom data file went into a blank run of it, and the engine played all three demos on the chip through a 16 kB page cache with the emulator's frame checksums: 21.9 frames per second (19.9 with an 8 kB cache). A 256-byte QSPI read takes 23.8 us.
rows.limits: Display and sound are stubbed. A 16 kB cache leaves 3 kB of RAM free. The real-time-paced rate was not measured.

rows.title: An MSP430 FRAM counter, ported to a part with no FRAM, survives resets and power-off
rows.says: A TI MSP430FR2433 persistent-variable example became an append-only log in one flash sector on the LP-MSPM0L1306. The count survived 17 software resets in a row, a new program load and a 5 s power-off; a flash word write takes 56 us and a sector erase 1.99 ms.
rows.limits: Nobody pressed the button, so the wake-from-sleep path is untested. The original was built for the MSP430FR2433 and never run: no MSP430 board on the bench.
rows.why: Code written for an MSP430 now runs on a newer, cheaper chip with no FRAM and still keeps its count after resets and power-off.

rows.title: The MSP430 FRAM counter, ported to the LP-MSPM33C321A, survives resets and a range-erase load
rows.says: The same persistent-counter example became a log of 16-byte slots in the last 2 kB sector of main flash on the LP-MSPM33C321A. The count rose by exactly 1 per software reset for 19 resets; a flash word write takes 80 us and a sector erase 2.59 ms. A program load that erases only the image's sectors kept the log; a plain full-erase load wiped it.
rows.limits: The build is a wait loop, so no button wake or sleep mode was tried, and power-off persistence was not measured. The original was built for the MSP430FR2433 and never run: no MSP430 board on the bench.
rows.why: Code written for an MSP430 keeps its count across resets on a third chip family member, as long as the program load does not erase the log's sector.

rows.title: The MSP430 FRAM counter, ported to a C2000 LAUNCHXL-F2800137, survives resets and a necessary-sectors load
rows.says: The persistent-counter example became a log of 64-bit slots in flash sector 100 on the LAUNCHXL-F2800137, written through the Flash API from RAM. The count rose by exactly 1 per software reset for 19 resets; a word write takes 64 us and a 2 kB sector erase 2.18 ms. DSLite set to erase necessary sectors only kept the log; its default entire-flash load and CCStudio's scripting runner erased it.
rows.limits: The build is a wait loop, so no button wake or sleep mode was tried, and power-off persistence was not measured. The original was built for the MSP430FR2433 and never run: no MSP430 board on the bench.
rows.why: An MSP430 persistent counter moves to a C2000 chip; the loader setting, not the code, decides whether the count survives a new program.

rows.title: An MSP430 LPM3 watchdog wake, ported to deep sleep on an LP-MSPM0L1306
rows.says: The 1 s watchdog wake from LPM3 became a watchdog interval timer in STANDBY0: a period of 0.9974 s over 29 ticks, with the CPU clock stopped (33.8 thousand SysTick ticks a second against 15.2 million in SLEEP). A 9600 baud UART echo from STANDBY0 returned 190 of 190 bytes of a burst on the bus clock.
rows.limits: No current meter, so no microamps. A UART on the 32 kHz clock lost most of a burst. The same idea on the LP-AM13E230 never woke and locked the debugger out.
rows.why: An MSP430 low-power wake-up routine moves to an MSPM0 and still wakes once a second.

rows.title: Doom plays its demos on the Educational BoosterPack screen of an LP-MSPM33C321A
rows.says: The rp2040-doom design draws a 128 x 96 window of the game to the BoosterPack screen through DMA at 16 MHz while reading its data file from the QSPI flash: 22.7 frames per second in real time with an 8 kB page cache (24.5 with 16 kB), the game running at its own 35 tics a second. A scripted player walked, turned and fired in E1M1 at about 31 frames per second.
rows.limits: Sound is compiled out. The stick and buttons were driven by a script, not a person (that row is waiting). Frame checksums were off in the real-time runs. A 16 kB cache leaves 151 bytes of RAM free.

rows.title: CHIP-8 test suite runs on the LP-MSPM0G3519 touch panel
rows.says: A CHIP-8 interpreter of about 200 lines of C draws the chip8-test-suite ROMs on the Waveshare 3.5 inch panel. The frame buffer on the board is byte for byte the host interpreter's for logo, IBM, Corax+, flags and quirks. Flat out it executes 526 thousand instructions per second, about 750 times a typical game's pace, and a full redraw takes 14.2 ms.
rows.limits: Nobody touched the key pad, so touch input is untested on the board. No sound. CHIP-8 only, not SUPER-CHIP or XO-CHIP. The suite is fetched, not stored.
rows.why: A set of retro CHIP-8 programs draws correctly on a small touch panel, so old games can run on it.

rows.title: A ZX Spectrum 48K runs BASIC on a Cortex-M0+ at a fifth of real speed
rows.says: The unmodified chips Z80 core and a small Spectrum machine run on the LP-MSPM0G3519 at 19.4 percent of a real Spectrum's speed with OpenSE BASIC idle and the core in SRAM (15.9 percent with the core in flash). After 400 emulated frames the screen memory on the board equals the host machine's, for a ROM-less test image and for BASIC. The CoreMark-scaled plan said 20 percent.
rows.limits: Real-time games and tape loading are out of reach by a factor of five; no sound, no contended memory timing. The touch keyboard was not pressed. The reader supplies the 16 kB ROM.
rows.why: A 1980s ZX Spectrum runs BASIC on a small Cortex-M0+ chip at about a fifth of real speed.

rows.title: An MP3 decodes bit-exact on the LP-MSPM33C321A at a sixth of real time
rows.says: minimp3 decodes a 5.07 s 128 kbps stereo clip in 0.151 times its length and a 64 kbps mono clip in 0.109 on the Cortex-M33 at 160 MHz with the hardware float unit. All 194 frame checksums equal the Mac's scalar build and the maximum sample error is 0.
rows.limits: Decode only; no audio was played. minimp3 has no fixed-point path. The LP-MSPM0G3519 result is its own milestone.
rows.why: An MP3 file decodes exactly right in about a sixth of real time, so the chip has room left for other work.

rows.title: A Lisp prompt runs on the LP-MSPM0G5187 from an unmodified Arduino sketch
rows.says: uLisp ARM 4.9a gives a Lisp prompt on the kit's serial port in 98.8 kB of flash and 23.1 kB of RAM. All 19 REPL checks pass, an endless recursion ends in an error message and the next line still runs, and (tak 18 12 6) takes 7.5 s at 80 MHz, (fib 23) 5.2 s and (q2 7 8) 19.2 s. The same source builds for the LP-MSPM0G3507 and LP-MSPM0G3519.
rows.limits: No analog read, no sound, SPI and I2C are stubs, no save-image. The G3507 and G3519 images are built, not flashed. The blink check script printed FAIL on the LED run; the pin samples show 6 changes in 16.
rows.why: A Lisp prompt runs on the MSPM0G5187 from an unchanged Arduino sketch.

rows.title: A Lisp prompt runs on the LP-EM-CC2340R5 from the same Arduino sketch
rows.says: uLisp ARM 4.9a gives a Lisp prompt on the kit's serial port in 96.3 kB of flash and 24.0 kB of RAM with the 2,800-object workspace. All 19 REPL checks pass, an endless recursion ends in an error message and the next line still runs, and (tak 18 12 6) takes 10.8 to 10.9 s at 48 MHz, (fib 23) 7.5 s and (q2 7 8) 28 s.
rows.limits: TI Arm Clang needs two changes the GCC build did not: a strcasecmp definition and an explicit read of the stack pointer, without which the stack guard never fired. No analog read, no sound, SPI and I2C are stubs, no save-image. The LED pin level was read back through the driver, not measured.
rows.why: The same Lisp interpreter runs on a Cortex-M0+ radio chip with a different compiler and SDK.

rows.title: A Lisp prompt runs on the LP-EM-CC2755P10 from the same Arduino sketch
rows.says: uLisp ARM 4.9a gives a Lisp prompt on the kit's serial port in 94.4 kB of flash and 24.2 kB of RAM with the 2,800-object workspace. All 19 REPL checks pass in each of three runs, and (tak 18 12 6) takes 3.1 to 3.2 s at 96 MHz, (fib 23) 2.2 s and (q2 7 8) 8.1 s: 3.4 times faster than the CC2340R5 for twice the clock.
rows.limits: The LED pin level was read back through the driver, not measured. No analog read, no sound, SPI and I2C are stubs, no save-image. An endless recursion ends in 'Error: no room' because the workspace fills before the 137 kB stack, so the stack guard did not fire. Arduino and MicroPython through TI's Zephyr fork did not build.
rows.why: The same Lisp interpreter runs on a Cortex-M0+ radio chip with a different compiler and SDK.

rows.title: A Lisp prompt runs on the LP-MSPM33C321A from the same Arduino sketch
rows.says: uLisp ARM 4.9a gives a Lisp prompt on the kit's serial port in 87.7 kB of flash and 23.2 kB of RAM with the 2,800-object workspace. All 19 REPL checks pass in each of three runs, the stack guard fires, and (tak 18 12 6) takes 2.5 to 2.6 s at 160 MHz, (fib 23) 1.7 s and (q2 7 8) 6.5 s: 1.2 times faster than the CC2755P10's Cortex-M33 at 96 MHz for 1.67 times the clock.
rows.limits: The LED pin level was read back through the GPIO input register, not measured. No analog read, no sound, SPI and I2C are stubs, no save-image. The time missed the clock-scaled figure by 37 percent; the flash wait states are the suspected cause, not measured.
rows.why: The same Lisp interpreter runs on a second Cortex-M33 with a different SDK and clock.

rows.title: The LE Audio codec (LC3) encodes and decodes bit-exact on the LP-MSPM33C321A
rows.says: liblc3 v1.1.3 encodes 16 kHz, 24 kHz and 48 kHz mono 10 ms frames in 197,885, 249,279 and 387,683 cycles on the Cortex-M33 at 160 MHz (12.4 to 24.2 percent of real time) and decodes them in 73,459, 114,018 and 168,113 (4.6 to 10.5 percent). The CRC-32 of every encoded frame and decoded block equals the Mac build in all three configurations. With the float unit off the same core needs 120 to 262 percent of real time to encode.
rows.limits: Codec only: a generated test signal, mono, 100 frames per configuration, no radio, no Bluetooth link and no audio output. The build is 157.8 kB of flash with every feature, 83.2 kB with LC3 only at -Os.
rows.why: The Bluetooth LE Audio codec encodes and decodes correctly using about an eighth of the chip's time.

rows.title: LC3 built for a Cortex-M0+ needs more than one core at 80 MHz
rows.says: liblc3 for a Cortex-M0+ (soft float) links to 135.6 kB of flash and 19.1 kB of static RAM, and ten frames run bit-exact in a Cortex-M0 emulator. The 16 kHz encode costs 2.63 million cycles a frame, 329 percent of real time at 80 MHz.
rows.limits: A model: the emulator prices instructions and has no flash stalls, so the numbers are a floor. Not flashed or run on a board.
rows.why: A Cortex-M0+ at 80 MHz is too slow for LE Audio on one core, so you know to pick a bigger chip before you design around it.

rows.title: An MP3 decodes bit-exact on the LP-MSPM0G3519 at 80 MHz, but at 9.8 times real time
rows.says: minimp3 decodes the 128 kbps stereo clip in 9.84 times its length and the 64 kbps mono clip in 7.38 on the Cortex-M0+ at 80 MHz with soft float, and all 194 frame checksums of each clip equal the Mac's scalar build (two runs). A Cortex-M0+ with no float unit would need about 787 MHz for stereo. The emulator model had said 7.7 to 10.7 and 5.8 to 7.9; the board used 1.27 times the modelled cycles.
rows.limits: Decode only; no audio was played. The timer is SysTick plus an overflow count, checked against delay_cycles (3 ppm) and the host clock (within 0.5 percent). The image is 150.3 kB of flash with 121.6 kB of clips and 34.1 kB of static RAM plus a 32 kB stack.
rows.why: MP3 decodes correctly on the MSPM0G3519 but about ten times too slowly for live playback, so you know to pick a faster chip.

rows.title: Plaits synthesis runs bit-exact on the LP-MSPM33C321A, 24 engines, a quarter of real time
rows.says: Mutable Instruments' Plaits code (MIT) renders a fixed note sequence through all 24 engines in 12-sample blocks at 48 kHz on the Cortex-M33 at 160 MHz. The CRC-32 of every block equals the Mac build for all 24 engines. A block costs 4.3k cycles (chiptune) to 13.8k (modal): 10.7 to 34.5 percent of real time, median 26.2, and 23 of 24 engines stay under 37 percent in every block. With the FPU off the same core needs 149 to 1,140 percent.
rows.limits: Synthesis only: render to RAM, no DAC, MIDI, CV or listening test; one voice and one fixed note sequence. The speech engine has three blocks at 166, 263 and 621 percent where the harmonics jump. Flash is 202.2 kB at -O2 (1 kB = 1,024 bytes).
rows.why: A full synthesizer with 24 sound engines runs on the MSPM33 at about a quarter of real time.

rows.title: Opus (libopus 1.5.2) encodes and decodes bit-exact on the LP-MSPM33C321A in fixed point
rows.says: libopus 1.5.2 fixed-point builds encode and decode 16 kHz voice (SILK), 48 kHz music (CELT, 10 and 20 ms) and 16 kHz CELT at complexity 0, 5 and 10; packets and decoded PCM equal a Mac build with the same multiply macros in 12 of 12 runs at three optimization levels. At 160 MHz CELT 48 kHz 10 ms encodes in 29 to 54 percent and decodes in 17 to 22 percent of real time; SILK decodes in 5 percent and encodes in 56 percent at complexity 0 (246 at 5, not real time).
rows.limits: Mono, constant bit rate, a generated signal, no radio or audio output. A Mac build with its default 64-bit multiply macros differs from CELT complexity 5 up. The float build runs but is slower in all 12 runs, and its decoded samples equal the Mac in 2 of 12. Flash 331.4 kB at -O2, 164.7 kB at -Os.
rows.why: The Opus audio codec encodes and decodes correctly on the MSPM33 in fixed-point math.

rows.title: LC3 frame lengths, packet loss concealment and two channels run bit-exact on the LP-MSPM33C321A
rows.says: liblc3 at 7.5, 5 and 2.5 ms frames (LC3plus for the last two) encodes in 13.5 to 34.1 percent and decodes in 4.8 to 16.8 percent of real time at 160 MHz, bit-exact against the Mac strict build in 9 of 9 runs. A concealed frame (every 10th frame lost) costs 43 to 58 percent of a good frame, and two channels at 48 kHz cost 2.00 times mono.
rows.limits: Mono except the stereo run, one second of generated signal, whole-run CRC-32 checks; no radio or audio output.
rows.why: LE Audio works with all three frame lengths, lost packets and two channels, so it covers real streaming cases.

rows.title: A BoosterPack sensor stream runs at 100 Hz with no gaps on the LP-MSPM0G5187
rows.says: The BP-BASSENSORSMKII pack's hall sensor (DRV5055), temperature and humidity sensor (HDC2080) and light sensor (OPT3001) stream in the dataset format at 100.00 Hz for 65.3 s: 6,528 rows, 0 gaps, 0 overruns. At rest the hall sensor reads 1,638.1 mV (sd 0.9), the temperature 21.66 C and the light 3,403 lux.
rows.limits: Rest only: no motion. The pack's BMI160 motion sensor does not answer at 0x68 or 0x69 although the HDC2080 on the same bus does, cause not found, so the 100 Hz motion dataset waits. The pack's TMP117 is dropped (its ribbon cable cannot be reseated). The magnet test was not run.
rows.why: A sensor BoosterPack streams readings at a steady 100 per second with no gaps.
rows.image_alt: The Sensors BoosterPack on an LP-MSPM0G5187

rows.title: The Doom image for the LP-EM-CC35X1 builds with a 3.5 inch panel driver
rows.says: An optional ST7796S driver (SPI at 16 MHz, DMA bands) links and signs as PANEL=1 build.sh 31: 2,084,118 B of flash (6.8 kB more) and 506,082 B of RAM, with a 31 kB zone. The wire list uses 9 wires with no collision with the ad blocker or the debug connector. The default image is byte-identical to before.
rows.limits: Built, not run: no wire is placed. Color order, short polled transfers and the frame rate are unproven; the SPI wire time predicts 10 to 18 frames per second, not the 39 of the no-panel image. No keys, sound or touch.

rows.title: Zephyr prints hello world on the AM62L's A53 from on-chip SRAM with the DDR never initialized
rows.says: A 124 KB Zephyr image in the 144 KB of SRAM at 0x707F0000, loaded over JTAG with the DDR never initialized, no TF-A and no TIFS, boots one A53 core at EL3 and prints its banner and the hello line on UART0 at 115200. The line rate was checked with a stream of 11.6 kB/s of clean 0x55 bytes.
rows.limits: JTAG load only: the boot ROM has not accepted the image as its phase-1 payload. One core, UART0 only. No speed, boot-time or power number.
rows.why: A Zephyr program boots on the AM62L's main core from on-chip memory before the external DDR RAM is set up.

rows.title: Linux and Zephyr run side by side on the AM62L's two A53 cores with no hypervisor
rows.says: Linux 6.18.38 from TI's SDK ran on core 0 (maxcpus=1) while a 45,092-byte Zephyr image in DDR ran on core 1, started by a PSCI CPU_ON call at non-secure EL1. Three minutes after Linux came up it read Zephyr's console ring through /dev/mem: 66 new bytes in 3 s, ticks 269 and 270, no SError, Oops or stall in dmesg.
rows.limits: Zephyr was started from U-Boot, not by Linux, and only its own timer ran: no interrupt from Linux, no shared peripheral, no message in either direction, cpuidle was off, no Linux reboot with Zephyr running. The on-chip SRAM is not usable beside Linux (TF-A's stub, a firewall). No timing or power number.
rows.why: An RTOS can run on one core of the AM62L beside Linux on the other with no hypervisor, which TI documents with Jailhouse.

rows.title: TI's Jailhouse hypervisor partitions the AM62L's two A53 cores: bare-metal demos and a second Linux run beside the first
rows.says: With the Jailhouse kernel, device tree and tools from TI's SDK 12.01.00.05.03 image on a USB stick, jailhouse enable took 0.27 s. The uart-demo and gic-demo inmates printed on UART1 within a second of the cell start (gic-demo: 359 timer samples, jitter 764 to 16,919 ns), and a second Linux 6.18.38 from a 142 MB RAM filesystem reached a login on UART1 about 20 s after its cell start while the first Linux stayed up on core 0. Stop, destroy and disable returned 0.
rows.limits: TI's demos only: no Zephyr or FreeRTOS cell, no message between cells, no latency under load, no power figure. Booted from a USB stick, not TI's micro-SD. The root cell logged an SCMI timeout on each cell create and destroy.
rows.why: TI's documented way to run an RTOS beside Linux on the AM62L works on the evaluation module as published.

rows.title: The AM62L decodes a 1080p H.264 camera stream in software on one A53 core
rows.says: ffmpeg 8.0.1 from TI's SDK image decoded a 1920x1080 baseline stream capped at 600 kbit/s at 34.0 fps on one A53 core at 1.25 GHz (50.2 on two), and a 540x540 stream at 172 fps. Main profile at 1080p ran 23.5 fps on one core, 35.5 on two. The repo's plain-C h264bsd decoder, built on the board, ran 540x540 at 97.5 fps, 2.9 times the AM263P. MD5 and CRC of every decoded frame equal the Mac's on all 9 streams.
rows.limits: Decode only: no scaling, no display and no LVGL beside it. Test-pattern streams; real camera footage at the same bitrate costs more. No power figure. One board.
rows.why: A 1080p baseline camera stream fits on one A53 core of the AM62L with no video block, so a design at that size needs no separate video chip.

rows.title: The frl tool backs up, builds, writes and checks a blink on the LP-MSPM0G3519 and LP-MSPM0C1104, as on the LP-MSPM0L1306
rows.says: Each board got a route in data/routes.json from its measured board facts (chip ID, main flash, LED pins). frl backed up main flash (read twice), built TI's gpio_toggle_output with the asked pattern (10.0 s and 8.9 s), wrote and read back the image (0.9 s and 1.0 s) and timed the LED through the debugger to 150, 150, 150, 900 ms; restore matched on read-back.
rows.limits: One board each, one day, built with SysConfig 1.28.0 where the route validates 1.26.3. The other bench boards (LP-MSPM0G5187, LP-MSPM33C321A, LP-AM13E230, the CC23xx and CC27xx kits) have no frl route.
rows.why: One local command takes two more LaunchPad kits from source to a checked LED, with a backup first and no CCStudio.

rows.title: The frl tool backs up, builds, writes and checks a blink on the LP-MSPM0G5187 and, through TI's OpenOCD, on the Cortex-M33 LP-MSPM33C321A
rows.says: The LP-MSPM0G5187 route runs on xPack OpenOCD like the other MSPM0 kits (write and read-back 0.8 s). The LP-MSPM33C321A route names TI's OpenOCD (CCSTUDIO-OPENOCD, from github.com/TexasInstruments/ti-openocd), which has the MSPM33 flash driver xPack OpenOCD lacks; frl finds it like any other tool. Both backed up first, timed the LED to 150, 150, 150, 900 ms and restored with a read-back match.
rows.limits: One board each, one day. The G5187 was built with SysConfig 1.28.0 where the route validates 1.26.3. The MSPM33C321A ran on a ti-release build at commit cb22a31e, not the packaged CCSTUDIO-OPENOCD 1.5.0 download.
rows.why: Four more LaunchPad kits (five with the LP-MSPM0L1306) go from source to a checked LED with one local tool and no CCStudio.

rows.title: The frl tool backs up, builds, writes and checks a blink on the LP-AM13E230, through TI's OpenOCD
rows.says: TI's AM13E230x SDK ships its examples without a makefile, so frl builds this one the way the SDK's CCStudio project does: SysConfig, TI Arm Clang and the SDK's prebuilt libraries (tools/frl/build_am13.py). TI's OpenOCD writes it (1.3 s with read-back) and frl times LED4 to 150, 150, 150, 900 ms, after a 512 kB backup; restore matched on read-back. The route accepts the production DEVICEID from the datasheet (PARTNUM 0x0BBE) and the prototype's (0x0000).
rows.limits: One prototype board (XAM13E23019), one day. A production board has not been seen; its ID is from the datasheet. TI's product page lists the part as Preview.
rows.why: A Cortex-M33 motor-control part TI ships without a makefile goes from source to a checked LED with one local tool and no CCStudio.

rows.title: The frl tool names, backs up, builds, writes and checks a blink on the C2000 LAUNCHXL-F2800137, with no OpenOCD
rows.says: OpenOCD cannot drive a C28x core, so the C2000 route runs every step through TI's CCStudio scripting: PARTIDH names the chip (0x06FF0500, TMS320F2800137), a 256 kB backup is read twice, TI's LED example is built for flash with the pattern (4.2 s), written and checked against the image (9.4 s), and LED4 is timed to 150, 150, 150, 900 ms; restore matched on read-back. With a debugger attached the C2000 waits in its boot ROM, so frl starts the program at the flash entry point the way a flash boot would.
rows.limits: One board, one day. CCStudio reads the pin about 42 times a second while the CPU runs, so the timing tolerance is 48 ms, against 40 ms on the Arm kits. Needs CCStudio installed.
rows.why: A C2000 joins the same one-command cycle as the Arm LaunchPad kits, through TI's own tools.

rows.title: The frl tool writes your message to the LP-EM-CC2340R5 and checks it on the serial port, three times back to back
rows.says: TI's tools erase the whole CC2340R5 before a write, configuration area included, so frl saves main flash and the CCFG first, writes with DSLite (8.8 to 9.8 s), checks main flash against the image and then reads the message from the probe's serial port, because reading memory would stop the program. Three rounds passed; asked for a different message, the check failed. The restore writes main flash and the CCFG back in one load and matched on read-back.
rows.limits: One board, one day. Every write erases the whole chip; the saved copy puts it back. Needs DSLite (UniFlash or CCStudio) and a separate XDS110 probe.
rows.why: A Bluetooth LE chip whose memory reads stop the program joins the same backup, write, check and restore cycle.

rows.title: The frl tool changes the LED pattern on the LP-CC1354P10-1 and times it, three times back to back
rows.says: This chip can refuse the second debugger connect a DSLite load makes, so frl runs every step through CCStudio's Python scripting, one connect per step: backup of main flash and the CCFG, write of main flash only (7.4 to 34.6 s), and a pattern check from the program's own log of LED changes, because the LED pin cannot be read while the program runs. Three patterns passed; asked for a different one, the check failed. Every restore of main flash and the CCFG matched on read-back.
rows.limits: One board on an external LP-XDS110, one day. A refused connect needs the probe's USB power cycled (by hand, or by uhubctl on a switchable hub); it did not happen in these runs. Needs CCStudio and the SimpleLink CC13xx CC26xx SDK.
rows.why: A sub-GHz and Bluetooth LE chip that takes a debugger only once joins the same backup, write, check and restore cycle.

rows.title: The frl tool prints your message from the LP-EM-CC35X1 and checks it on the serial port, three times back to back
rows.says: frl edits TI's uart2echo, builds and signs it, programs it with TI's Wi-Fi Toolbox (23 to 24 s) and reads the message on the probe's serial port. This chip cannot be read back, so the backup keeps the fuse report and the running program's first line, and the restore programs a signed image you name and checks that line. Three messages passed; asked for another, the check failed. Four restores put the earlier program back.
rows.limits: One board, one day. No byte comparison is possible: the image on the board is unknown, and the restore is only as good as the image you name. The chip must be activated first; frl never touches its fuses.
rows.why: A Wi-Fi 6 chip with no read-back joins the same cycle, with an honest restore instead of a pretend backup.

rows.title: Zephyr's open MSPM0 I2C driver and a flash driver run on the LP-MSPM0G3519
rows.says: Zephyr's open I2C pull request (#117311) applies to Zephyr main without a conflict. On the board, a controller and Zephyr's EEPROM target on one I2C peripheral passed 12 of 12 checks (16-byte and 128-byte writes and reads, a register byte, an unused address gives an error), and the I2C scan found the touch controller of the wired Waveshare panel at 0x38 and read vendor ID 0x11 and chip ID 0x64. A flash driver derived from the open flash pull request (#91500) passed 18 of 18 checks on the last 1 kB sector: erase 2,625 us, write 1,024 bytes 8,676 us, 1,024 of 1,024 bytes read back equal through the debugger.
rows.limits: One board, 100 kHz only, polling flash driver. Neither driver is merged: #117311 has changes requested, #91500 conflicts with main, and the flash driver here is a rewrite of it. The Sensors BoosterPack (HDC2080) was not stacked on this board, and the LP-MSPM0G5187 has no board in Zephyr main. Data sheet erase and program times were not compared.
rows.why: Zephyr can talk I2C and write flash on MSPM0 once the two open pull requests land.

rows.title: MicroPython runs on an LP-EM-CC2340R5 through upstream's Zephyr port
rows.says: MicroPython 1.29.0 on Zephyr 4.4.2 gives a prompt on the probe's serial port, sets and reads a pin from Python, and reads an ADC pin (65,471 of 65,535 with the pin pulled up, 16 pulled down). The image is 174.8 kB of the 512 kB flash and 29.9 kB of the 36 kB RAM with a 20 kB Python heap. MicroPython's stock Zephyr settings overflow the RAM by 46.8 kB; one config file and one devicetree overlay fix it.
rows.limits: One board. The LED blink was not seen (the bench camera had no frame); pin read-back only. I2C, SPI, PWM and UART were not exercised. No file system, so scripts are pasted at the prompt.
rows.why: You can type Python at a prompt on a 36 kB Bluetooth chip with the same Zephyr port other boards use.

rows.title: Arduino's Blink and AnalogReadSerial run unchanged on an LP-EM-CC2340R5 and an LP-MSPM0G3519 through the Zephyr-based core
rows.says: Both stock examples build with no sketch edit and run on both boards, with one devicetree overlay of about 40 lines per board. Flash is 27.7 and 27.8 kB on the CC2340R5 and 22.8 kB on the G3519; RAM is 5.2 and 4.8 kB. The notebook's own layer builds Blink at 2.6 kB on the G3507 but cannot build AnalogReadSerial because it has no analogRead.
rows.limits: One board of each. The core's Serial drops bytes at 9600 baud unless a six-line patch is applied. The G3519 needs Zephyr main for its ADC driver and an nRST pulse after flashing. Wire, SPI, tone and interrupts were not run. LED blink read through the GPIO output register, not seen.
rows.why: Arduino sketches with analogRead and Serial run on these two TI boards without an Arduino layer of their own.

rows.title: Mosquitto, Node-RED, Pi-hole and Home Assistant Container run on the AM62L from TI's own Linux image, and Python GPIO toggles its LED
rows.says: TI's SDK 12.01 Linux image already carries Docker 29.3.0, so the four arm64 containers ran as published. Each did one real thing: an MQTT message crossed the broker both ways, a Node-RED flow answered an HTTP call, Pi-hole answered 0.0.0.0 for three ad hosts, and an MQTT sensor reading 21.5 appeared in Home Assistant 2026.10.4. Home Assistant needs 557 MiB and 67.7 s to answer its first API call; the other three need 3 to 110 MiB.
