Board power stayed within 5 mW of 568 mW. gpiozero (lgpio) and Adafruit Blinka (with a new AM62L board file) toggle the user LED's output register.
rows.limits: One board, one run per app. The user button press was not recorded, and the LED was checked by register, not by eye. Python GPIO took three workarounds (lgpio build, gpiozero board description, Blinka board entry). Package installs through opkg do not work outside TI's network. Zigbee2MQTT and Frigate were not run.
rows.why: The software most people run on a Raspberry Pi runs on the AM62L without changing the operating system.

rows.title: Interrupts, PWM, SPI and I2C run through Arduino-on-Zephyr and MicroPython-on-Zephyr on the LP-EM-CC2340R5 and LP-MSPM0G3519
rows.says: On the CC2340R5, attachInterrupt and Pin.irq counted 10 of 10 software-triggered edges, analogWrite and machine.PWM set the timer registers as expected, SPI.transfer and machine.SPI completed, and Wire and machine.I2C scanned the bus. On the G3519, Wire read the touch controller at 0x38 through the Zephyr MSPM0 I2C driver 100 of 100 times (489 us a read), SPI loopback returned 256 of 256 bytes through the SPI block's loopback bit, attachInterrupt and analogWrite ran. Images 31 to 38 kB of flash.
rows.limits: CC2340R5 SPI data unchecked (no loopback wire) and no I2C device was on the bus; the LED was not seen. Four upstream faults found: the CC23 GPIO driver clears edge detect on any reconfigure; the CC2340R5 board file maps the red PWM LED to the wrong timer channel; MicroPython duty_u16 overflows at 1 kHz (one-cast patch verified); the shared MSPM0 pin file is wrong for the G351x (PB27 proven, 136 of 443 entries differ by data), the MSPM0 GPIO driver never clears old edge bits, the MSPM0 PWM driver inverts duty, and the core's transfer(buf, n) splits write and read.
rows.why: The four peripheral families an Arduino or MicroPython program needs are proven on both boards, so a sketch or script that uses them has a measured path here.

rows.title: Renesas FSP examples run on an LP-MSPM0G3519 with their application source unchanged
rows.says: Four examples from Renesas ra-fsp-examples (BSD-3-Clause) ran on the G3519 through a 577-line layer that maps FSP HAL calls onto DriverLib: the UART, ADC single-scan and GPT timer examples with no source edit (timer PWM 0.89 to 100.00 percent high at 1 kHz), and the I2C controller example with five constants changed to read the touch controller on this bench instead of the accelerometer it ships for. The timer-triggered ADC example also runs unchanged on the MSPM0 event fabric (1,023 intervals within 2 counts of target, none missed). 12.4 to 15.5 kB of flash.
rows.limits: One board. The layer is written driver code, not a rename shim. The timer-triggered ADC example's two-group DMA chain fills the first group at half rate and never finishes the second (measured on the board). The timer runs 0.55 percent short against the Mac clock (the internal oscillator). The ADC pin was floating. Other vendors' example code is licensed to their own chips and is ported by behavior only.
rows.why: Code written for a Renesas FSP project has a measured path to an MSPM0 part: which files move untouched and how big the layer is.

rows.title: Raspberry Pi Pico SDK examples run on an LP-MSPM0G3519 with their source unchanged
rows.says: Five pico-examples (serial hello, I2C bus scan, blink, PWM fade, ADC read) build and run with no edit to their .c files on a 316-line layer that provides the Pico SDK's stdlib, gpio, uart, i2c, pwm, adc and time calls over DriverLib. The bus scan finds the touch controller at 0x38 and nothing else, 3 of 3. 1.8 to 10.6 kB of flash.
rows.limits: One board. The layer is written driver code (PORTING.md rule 3). The LED was not watched; the PWM fade rate is computed, not measured; the ADC input was floating. No PIO: programs that need Raspberry Pi's programmable I/O have no equivalent here.
rows.why: Pico SDK code written for the RP2040 has a measured path to an MSPM0 part, with the layer files listed for copying into another project.

rows.title: MicroPython runs on the LP-MSPM33C321A through Zephyr with its own unmodified settings
rows.says: MicroPython 1.29.0's Zephyr port links with its shipped prj.conf in 292.3 kB of the chip's 1 MB of flash and 83.6 kB of its 256 kB of RAM, a 48 kB Python heap. The REPL, Pin, float and SPI calls run on the board.
rows.limits: Needs Zephyr main plus two open TI pull requests (UART and clock, GPIO); the released Zephyr board has no UART or GPIO. I2C reads hang the console; Zephyr has no ADC or PWM driver for this chip. A Python loop pass takes 5.0 us, cause not found. One board, LED not watched, SPI data unchecked.
rows.why: MicroPython has a measured path onto TI's Cortex-M33 LaunchPad, with the pinned Zephyr tree and the files to rebuild it.

rows.title: Jack-o'-Lantern Jukebox: a LaunchPad and the Audio BoosterPack play a Halloween music and light show from a power bank
rows.says: The LP-MSPM33C321A plays five public-domain orchestral recordings and four synth arrangements on a loop through the BOOSTXL-AUDIO, with scare sounds, four effect modes, seven RGB light themes and two-button controls, and starts by itself on a USB power bank. 16,000 samples a second with no bad frames; a speaker EQ fitted from a sweep makes music 3.2 dB louder.
rows.limits: The pack's microphone has no power on this LaunchPad, so the clap and word triggers are not on it. Loudness stops rising above software volume step 10 of 16, measured with a laptop microphone; whether the amplifier, the speaker or the microphone flattens it was not separated. Sound and buttons were checked by the board's own logs and a laptop microphone, plus the owner's listening.
rows.why: A small project a reader can build in an evening from a LaunchPad and one BoosterPack, with the files and the button card.

rows.title: Models ran on the AM13E230 straight from the training tool's file: float, TFLite, trees, and an int8 of our own
rows.says: Four float32 CNNs exported by torch, a Keras CNN as float32 and int8 TFLite, a scikit-learn decision tree and random forest, and an XGBoost model went to portable C with tools/byom (Python 3.10 or newer, no package to install) and gave the training tool's class on 20 of 20 held-out windows on the LP-AM13E230 for every float and tree model. Float as trained runs at 0.392 to 22.48 ms, tuned loops at 0.302 to 13.57 ms, and the tool's own int8 (a documented scheme with a calibration set) keeps 79 of 80 answers at 0.447 to 19.95 ms, within 1.2 times the vendor's int8 CPU code. The XGBoost model is the most accurate of the nine and takes 80 us. With CMSIS-NN kernels behind the same front end the 8k model takes 2.894 ms and the 30k 8.540 ms, faster than the vendor's NPU build on the 30k.
rows.limits: Plain C reaches 4.4 to 7 cycles per multiply-add here; a kernel library is the next rung. The NPU build of the vendor's int8 models stays 4.6 times faster than CMSIS-NN on the 8k model and needs the vendor's quantization scheme; on the 30k model it leaves a layer on the CPU and loses to CMSIS-NN. The int8 TFLite file is read on the float path and matches its interpreter on 15 of 20; that file had already lost 9 points of accuracy in its own conversion. Times are the fastest of 20 vectors, model call only, one dataset.
rows.why: The question every engineer with a trained model asks first: does it run as it is, how fast, and does it still give my answers.

rows.number: 60 fps at 1080p, SNES and PlayStation tests
rows.title: The AM62L runs SNES and PlayStation emulator cores at 60 fps on HDMI with no X server and no container
rows.says: Snes9x 2005 holds 60 fps at 640x480, 800x600, 1280x720 and 1920x1080 on free homebrew programs, using 2.5 to 3.6 ms of each 16.7 ms frame, with audio and with a video thread. PCSX-ReARMed holds 60 fps on a PlayStation GPU test program at 3.6 ms a frame. The Game Boy core that gave 48 fps in the showcase gives 60 fps in the same modes: the earlier loss was X, the container and software OpenGL scaling, not the cores.
rows.limits: Free homebrew and test programs only, which are lighter than many commercial titles; the PlayStation load stayed at 100 flat triangles (pad input did not register); the display controller has no plane scaler, so the CPU scales; the monitor was not photographed.
rows.why: A no-GPU board can run retro emulation at full speed when the emulator draws straight to the display.

rows.title: The IWRL6432BOOST tracks and counts a person live in a browser from a config file on its shipped image
rows.says: On the shipped Presence_Demo image (SDK 05.04.00.01) a people-tracking config sent over the serial port gives a live top-down room view. On a spoken-cue walk (far wall, back, side to side, seated 15 s, wave, leave) one person was counted right in 89.5 percent of in-view frames with no frame showing two; TI's tracker lines alone gave 25.2 percent because a track left at the far wall lingered.
rows.limits: One person, one run, board flat on a desk about 1 m up; 250 ms frames because 100 ms hung the image; a track starts only after the person moves.
rows.why: Occupancy and meeting-room sensing needs a count, not just a presence flag, and this radar gives one with no new firmware.

rows.title: The AM62L's Linux glue file builds and runs unchanged on the BeagleY-AI, and one app picks the C7x or the Arm cores at run time
rows.says: The portable app's glue_linux.c (66 lines) built byte-identical with the BeagleY-AI's own gcc and ran 14 lines at one per second, needing only a 2-line config header; the AM62L's atomics shim and moonlight-embedded build rebuilt with no edits. A 23-line app with a 59-line glue file classified frames at 30.1 fps using the C7x and software decode, against 10.1 fps on the Arm cores, with the classifier alone 11.6 times faster.
rows.limits: The board has no ADC, so the app printed 65535 on every line; the LED was not seen. The hardware video decoder finished 4 runs and failed 7, so the 30.1 fps figure uses software decode. The AM62L side of the accelerator seam was not run. Nothing was built for the chip's R5F cores.
rows.why: A Linux glue file written for one board is the unit that moves to the next, and the accelerator is the new seam to cut.

rows.title: MLPerf Tiny keyword spotting runs on the LP-MSPM0G5187's NPU in 18.7 ms at 91.0 percent on the full test split; ResNet-8 does not fit
rows.says: TI's DS-CNN keyword spotter from the MLPerf Tiny benchmark runs 53.5 inferences a second on the NPU at 80 MHz (18.70 ms, all 11 compute layers on the NPU, 67.6 kB flash) and gets 91.0 percent of the 4,890 test clips right; ST's published Cortex-M33 result at 96 MHz is 48.4 ms and its accelerator build 16.5 ms.
rows.limits: Not an official submission: the MLPerf Tiny UART runner pass has not run on this board, and the first 1,000 clips score 89.7 percent, 0.3 points under the closed-division bar of 90, and two runs of TI's quantization-aware training did not clear it (89.6 and 89.0 percent on the host, 88.9 on the board). The CPU build does not link (43.7 kB of data against 32 kB RAM) and ResNet-8 does not fit.
rows.why: The maker-default open FOC library had no TI board; this is the port layer a maker needs, with the first numbers.

rows.number: 64.5 ms on the C7x, 184.6 ms on Frigate's CPU detector
rows.title: Frigate, the home camera recorder with no TI detector, runs its object detection on the BeagleY-AI's C7x through a 100-line server
rows.says: Frigate 0.18.2 on the board sent its detections through its DeepStack detector to a server running the zoo's yolox-nano on the C7x: 64.46 ms per detection and 6.6 a second with no frames dropped, against 184.56 ms, 4.5 a second and about 2 frames a second dropped on Frigate's own CPU detector, and 628.72 ms with the same model on the Arm cores. It tracked two people and a dog at 93, 84 and 83 percent.
rows.limits: One recorded clip, one run per row. The USB webcam as the input dropped off USB within seconds, 2 of 2 tries, so no camera-in-the-loop number. One camera, no recording, no MQTT. Frigate's inference figure was 64.46 ms where 25 to 40 ms was expected.
rows.why: Frigate lists detectors for a dozen accelerators and none for TI's; this is the first run of one.

rows.number: 76.5 fps into a program, 135.1 fps transcode
rows.title: The BeagleY-AI's video decoder feeds a program at 76.5 frames a second once frames are scaled before the colour conversion
rows.says: Hardware H.264 decode into a pipe looked broken: runs stalled, crashed or timed out. The cause was order: converting the full 1280x768 frame to RGB on the Arm cores read the decoder's slow buffers at 6.5 fps. Scaling to 224x224 first ran 300 frames in 3.92 s, 5 of 5 runs, and the seam app with the classifier on the C7x went from 6.4 to 61.3 fps. Chained decode and encode went from 35.1 to 135.1 fps at 1080p by letting the encoder import the decoder's buffers.
rows.limits: One board, one clip per test. Forcing an io-mode or threading videoconvert on the decoder's buffers crashes gst-launch-1.0. FFmpeg's hardware encoder still hangs.
rows.why: The decoder's own documentation does not say which element order a program reading frames needs.

rows.title: People counting on the BeagleY-AI's C7x runs at 30 frames a second to a browser, after three fixes to the stock app's start-up
rows.says: TI's Edge AI app with a people-count overlay detected and counted people in a recorded station clip at 30.0 fps (900 frames in 30 s) with the C7x 27 percent busy. Started over ssh it ran at 1.3 fps on the Arm cores: the app picks its accelerators from an SOC variable that only a login shell sets. Two more fixes: its stats screen needs a terminal (-n), and its detection decoder crashed on a frame with exactly one detection.
rows.limits: Recorded clip only: the USB webcam drops off USB on this board's supply, so no camera run. One board, no fan (75 to 79 C).
rows.why: The SOC variable is easy to miss: the app logs one warning and silently runs 25 times slower.

rows.number: pose 13 per second, drawing 5 to 6 fps
rows.title: Pop the bubbles plays on the BeagleY-AI with body pose on the C7x, and drawing is now the limit
rows.says: The body-pose game ran on a recorded clip of a walking person: pose on the C7x 13 times a second (59 ms inside the game, 43 ms for the bare model), both hands tracked, 22 bubbles popped in 40 s. The game redraws only 5 to 6 frames a second at 1280x720, 10.8 at 640x360: clip decoding, blending and drawing on the Arm cores, not the accelerator.
rows.limits: Recorded clip, no camera, no HDMI, no sound device tested. One board.
rows.why: A children's game needs about 20 frames a second; the numbers say where the work goes next.

rows.title: The radar people counter builds for all five chips of its family, and one cfg line breaks on the newer SDK
rows.says: TI's presence and tracking demo from MMWAVE-L-SDK 05.05.04.02 builds on a Mac for the IWRL6432/AWRL6432, IWRL6432AOP and IWRL1432/AWRL1432 variants, boot images included, within 192 B of TI's prebuilt images. The host code needs no change. Our cfg needs trackingCfg cut to four values on 05.05 on every chip, the AOP part needs its antenna map and TDM MIMO, and the 1432 parts move the chirp up 17 GHz.
rows.limits: Built, not flashed or run. 1432 antenna spacing not checked, so angles there are unknown. No AWRL, AOP or 1432 board.
rows.why: Shows what a builder changes to move the people counter to the automotive or 77 GHz parts before buying one.

rows.number: 1,696 of 1,696 points through the ROS driver at 50 ms frames, 0 at 250 ms
rows.title: The most-used open radar readers work on the IWRL6432BOOST's points once it sends the standard format, and the ROS driver needs frames under 100 ms
rows.says: With guiMonitor 1 the board sends the mmWave SDK 3 point layout. The most-forked Python SDK 3 reader then reads every point of two walk recordings unchanged (NumPy 1.26; on macOS a read-first port wrapper). The reference ROS 1 driver builds on Noetic with a C++14 edit and publishes every point identically when frames come every 50 ms, none at the board's 250 ms, because its reader adds a stale byte on each 100 ms timeout. The top gesture recognizer reads none of the stream: it wants its own AWR1642 SDK 2 layout and near-field gestures at 10 frames a second.
rows.limits: Replays of re-encoded real recordings; ROS not run live (Docker on macOS has no USB serial); live Python run with an empty room checked frames, not points.
rows.why: Tells a builder which popular radar code reads this board today, and the one cfg line and frame period it needs.

rows.number: 16 lines at 1.00 s on the MCU R5F
rows.title: The same app.c that runs on MSPM0 LaunchPad kits and under Linux runs on the BeagleY-AI's MCU R5F core, loaded from Linux
rows.says: Upstream Zephyr's beagley_ai/j722s/mcu_r5f0_0 board built the unchanged portable app into a 21,372-byte image that Linux started through remoteproc; it printed t=0 to t=15 one second apart into the remoteproc trace buffer and stopped on request. Three glue fixes made it work: re-enabling the MCU timer's compare after a posted write dropped it, mapping the mailbox page as device memory, and answering Linux's shutdown message.
rows.limits: One board. No ADC on the board, so every line reads adc=65535; the LED is not driven. After a stop the core starts again only after a reboot. The image must not use the core's default firmware name, or the boot loader starts it at every boot.
rows.why: It shows one C file moving from a microcontroller to the microcontroller-class core inside a Linux vision chip with only glue changed.

rows.title: CC35X1 speed-run batch: the control loop and security images still give no timed rows
rows.says: The trigger-by-ISR control image and the security image were flashed after a full flash erase. The control image reported its FOC step again (592.5 cycles) but the ADC interrupt never fired; the security image printed nothing in 900 s. The 124-cycle GPIO toggle (about 5 times the expectation) repeated.
rows.limits: One board. Rows for the control loop, ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SHA-256 and ECDSA stay failed after three tries each; H.264, dcache counters and hardware AES have no image.
rows.why: It records which timed rows the board does not yet give and why they were skipped.

rows.number: P63 29.8 fps with the camera; E294 0 of 5 starts held
rows.title: BeagleY-AI with its USB camera: the bubbles game runs, TI's people-count app reboots the board
rows.says: With the Insta360 Link 2 Pro attached, Pop the bubbles ran 20 s on the C7x pose model at 29.8 draw frames a second (pose 11.0 a second, model 57 ms). TI's camera people-count app streamed 29.9 fps for 5 s, then the board left Ethernet and rebooted; four of five camera starts did the same.
rows.limits: One board, wall supply of unread rating. Cause unknown: no console or power meter. P63 with a browser display also rebooted the board once; no camera frame was saved.
rows.why: It shows the camera demos work for seconds and records where they stop, so the next try changes the power, not the code.

rows.number: 2,931 CoreMark per second at 799.98 MHz; Zephyr blinky from RAM
rows.title: LP-AM243: TI and Zephyr programs run from RAM with the boot switches as shipped
rows.says: A debugger script loads any image to RAM in about 3 s with flash and switches untouched. CoreMark 3.664 per MHz across all four R5F cores one at a time, Dhrystone 1.941 DMIPS per MHz in TI's example, FOC step 245 cycles, interrupt latency 182 cycles. Upstream Zephyr hello_world and blinky run the same way.
rows.limits: One board. Ethernet and power not measured yet. GPIO stores take 147 cycles. No timed first blink.
rows.why: It shows the board is usable from a Mac as it comes out of the box, given a 3 A charger.

rows.number: 11,730 CoreMark per second on four R5F cores; 82 of 121 SDK examples print a pass
rows.title: LP-AM243: four cores at once, a newer compiler, the PRU and the SDK sweep
rows.says: CoreMark on all four R5F cores at once gives 2,931 to 2,933 per core, within 0.1% of one core alone. TI Arm Clang 5.1.1 (inside CCStudio) adds 7.5% on the same source. A PRU core writes its output register in 5.3 ns at a measured 200 MHz. 163 of 194 SDK example projects build from the terminal and 82 of the 121 R5FSS0-0 projects loaded printed a pass.
rows.limits: One board. TI's IPC example (3.19 us per round trip) started only once per power-up, so one run. The PRU pad rate was not seen. The sweep ran without a chip reset between examples, and three of its examples wrote ten bytes to the board EEPROM.
rows.why: It shows what the four cores deliver together and where the SDK examples stop working from a terminal.

rows.number: 10.1, 50.0 and 90.0% read against a true 10, 50 and 90
rows.title: LP-MSPM0L1306: reading a running chip from the browser
rows.says: Through the XDS110 and without stopping the program, Chrome reads CPU load, the running function, powered blocks, pin setup and pin changes about 500 times a second. The load readings match a test program with a known load.
rows.limits: Mapped for four MSPM0 chips (L1306, G3507, G3519, G5187); load checked against a known program only on the L1306. Pin changes above about 100 a second are too fast to count, and a program in deep sleep drops the debug link.
rows.why: It shows a running chip can be watched without changing its program.

rows.number: 10.1, 50.0 and 90.0% read against a true 10, 50 and 90
rows.title: LP-AM243: watching a running R5F core through the debug port
rows.says: Power, pads, pin changes and timer counts read from the running chip with no help from the program. CPU load needs a counter in the program, because the Cortex-R5 has no program counter sampler: with it, a FreeRTOS program read 29.99% for a task designed at 30%.
rows.limits: One board, one core, R5FSS0-0. Load, task load and interrupt enables need a change to the program.
rows.why: It shows what the debug port can read on the AM243 without touching the program, and what it cannot.

rows.number: 26.5 tokens a second at -O3 against 21.2 at -O2
rows.title: LP-MSPM33C321A: the Audio BoosterPack algorithms timed, and the story model faster with a compiler setting
rows.says: The pitch tracker, spectrum, DTMF decoder and noise gate with echo ran on the chip at 32 MHz with cycle counts of 356k, 72.1k, 51.0k and 104 a sample. The TinyStories model writes the same 128 token ids at 21.2, 26.5 and 25.9 tokens a second at -O2, -O3 and -Os.
rows.limits: The live microphone and speaker checks did not complete: no tone was heard by the firmware or by a Mac microphone. One board, one run of each compiler setting for the model.
rows.why: It gives the cycle budget of four audio algorithms on a Cortex-M33 and shows the compiler setting matters more than expected for int8 inference.

rows.number: 106 of 108 SDK example builds, 34 of 34 no-wiring runs started
rows.title: LP-EM-CC2340R5: the F3 SDK examples built and run by script
rows.says: 106 of 108 TI Arm Clang variants of the SDK's examples build from the terminal. 34 no-wiring variants (23 examples) flashed and started with no fault, and a PWM example's timer registers stepped through the expected duty values.
rows.limits: Started means serial text or pin registers seen, not each example's full behavior. 22 variants need wiring, 30 a second radio, 13 a phone or Mac peer. IAR and GCC variants not tried. One board.
rows.why: It shows which of TI's examples for this chip work from a Mac terminal and which need parts, so a reader knows where to start.

rows.title: LAUNCHXL-F2800137: backup, build, flash and LED check in one terminal command
rows.says: frl run took the board from a powered, identified LaunchPad to a changed blink in 58 s: the flash backed up and read twice, TI's blink example built, written to main flash through CCStudio scripting, and LED4 timed to 150, 150, 150 and 900 ms on the pin. The restore read back identical.
rows.limits: Terminal path only, from a board already powered and identified; no first-power clock and no tool install time. One run. Needs CCStudio and C2000Ware installed first.
rows.why: It shows how long the terminal path to a working C2000 blink takes once the tools are installed.

rows.title: LAUNCHXL-F2800137: print your own message from one terminal command
rows.says: frl run with the print-message recipe backed up the flash, built TI's launchxl_f2800137 demo with your words in it, wrote main flash in 11.2 to 14.0 s and read the message on the probe's serial port at 115200, three runs out of three. The restore read back identical.
rows.limits: Terminal path from a board already powered and identified; one probe; needs CCStudio and C2000Ware installed first. The listen is 4 s, so the counter reaches 3 or 4.
rows.why: It adds the F2800137 to the print-a-message project: text from a C2000 chip reaches the computer over the board's own USB cable.

rows.title: LP-MSPM0G3519: MicroPython pystone and a one-command blink
rows.says: The full MicroPython image on the LP-MSPM0G3519 ran a low-memory pystone at 1,112 pystones per second at 80 MHz (three runs, 1,111 to 1,114). frl run built, flashed and verified a changed blink on PB26 in 9.5 s warm and 30.0 s cold. The board was restored to its backup and read back identical.
rows.limits: The pystone script uses list records, so compare it only with itself. The blink time is terminal only, with no first-power clock, and ran on SysConfig 1.28.0, which the route does not validate.
rows.why: It gives the first MicroPython speed number and a repeatable setup time for this board.

rows.title: LP-MSPM0G5187: a one-command blink in 10 s
rows.says: frl run built, flashed and verified a changed blink on the LP-MSPM0G5187's red LED (PA17) in 10.1 s median of three runs (9.4 to 10.5 s), with the pin timed against the asked pattern each time. The blink image is 536 bytes of flash. The board was restored to its backup and read back identical.
rows.limits: Terminal only, with no first-power clock; all three runs were warm, so there is no cold-run time. It ran on SysConfig 1.28.0, which the route does not validate. uLisp analogread and save-image are not run: the port has no ADC or flash-storage code.
rows.why: It gives a repeatable setup time for this board and closes the stale not-run rows.

rows.title: CC35X1 check: board on its Sparky image, presence lab image held back by the preflight
rows.says: The board answers at 115200 and its banner after a reset reads 0.0.33.0, the image with a saved signed bundle. The Wi-Fi presence lab image exists but the image preflight refuses its single-slot layout against the two-slot reference, so it was not programmed.
rows.limits: One board. No smoke session and no labelled session ran; the lab rows stay not_run, and the labelled ones need a person in the room.
rows.why: It records that the lab image is ready but gated, and what the gate compares.

rows.title: Digital Lab in Chrome on the LP-MSPM0G3519: connect, write and read back, put back
rows.says: With Chrome's WebHID device policy granting the probe to the page, the Digital Lab connected to the board, wrote nine demos and passed its own check on seven, and its Put back restored the saved copy and read it back equal in 30 s.
rows.limits: One board, Chrome 156 on macOS 26.5, policy instead of the chooser, Web Serial through a stand-in. The Breathing LED check failed, Button to LED needs a hand on S2, and unplug-and-reconnect was not tested.
rows.why: It is the first real-Chrome run of the page for the MSPM0 family, with its one failed check recorded.

rows.title: Digital Lab in Chrome on the LP-MSPM0L1306: connect, write and read back, put back
rows.says: With Chrome's WebHID device policy granting the probe to the page, the Digital Lab connected to the board, wrote all eight demos and passed its own check on each, and its Put back restored the saved copy and read it back equal in 14 s.
rows.limits: One board, Chrome 156 on macOS 26.5, policy instead of the chooser, Web Serial through a stand-in. The mouse-drawn digit and the Copy buttons did not run, and unplug-and-reconnect was not tested.
rows.why: It is the first real-Chrome run of the page on the board the page was written for, with no failed check.

rows.number: 3 of 3 message runs passed, 28 to 30 s each
rows.title: LP-MSPM33C321A: print your own message from one command
rows.says: One frl command backed up the board, put a message in TI's UART console example, built it in 3.2 to 4.2 s, wrote it in 0.7 to 0.8 s and read the message on the probe's serial port. Three runs back to back passed and the first backup restored with the flash read back equal.
rows.limits: One board, one probe, an Intel Mac. TI's example sends five lines and stops, so the check counted 3, 4 and 4 copies.
rows.why: It adds the MSPM33C321A to the print-a-message project with the same route the MSPM0L1306 and CC2340R5 use.

rows.number: ML-KEM-768 in 42 ms and ML-DSA-44 signing in 514 ms on 36 kB of RAM
rows.title: Post-quantum key exchange and signatures run on the LP-EM-CC2340R5 with code written for another chip
rows.says: The portable ML-KEM-768 and ML-DSA-44 code that first ran on the CC1354P10 runs on the LP-EM-CC2340R5 (Cortex-M0+, 48 MHz, 36 kB RAM) and passes every NIST known-answer test. ML-KEM-768 key pair, encapsulate and decapsulate take 42, 50 and 61 ms at -Os; ML-DSA-44 built with the low-RAM option takes 141 ms to make a key pair, 514 ms to sign one message and 164 ms to verify. Three flashes agree within 1 part in 10,000.
rows.limits: Random bytes came from a fixed-seed generator because the CC23x0 has no general-purpose TRNG. The join with a Mac was not run. ML-DSA-44 signing time varies from 307 ms to 2.5 s across 16 messages. ML-DSA-44 was built at -Os only.
rows.why: Encryption designed to resist future quantum computers fits and runs on a 36 kB radio chip.

rows.number: 680 to 794 pystones per second at 80 MHz on 72.9 kB of flash
rows.title: MicroPython boots on the LP-MSPM0G5187
rows.says: The notebook's MicroPython port gained a G5187 build (UART block UC0, pin table from SysConfig data). The minimal image flashed as a raw binary, printed the MicroPython banner on the backchannel UART, reported machine.freq() 80000000 with 28,992 B of heap free, and toggled machine.Pin A17 and A24 (read through the debug port). Pystone ran 3 times on a 4 kB-stack build.
rows.limits: The minimal level only: the full image is 47,012 B too big for the 128 kB flash. The minimal level has no slice syntax and its 1.5 kB stack stops the benchmark, so the pystone numbers come from a slice-free copy of the script on a 4 kB-stack build. No hardware SPI, I2C or ADC in the port.
rows.why: It adds a third MSPM0 part to the MicroPython port and shows what the 32 kB parts give up.

rows.number: Blink and a serial sketch run; PA17 half periods 1,000 and 500 ms
rows.title: The Arduino compatibility layer runs on the LP-MSPM0G5187
rows.says: A new board folder builds the Arduino layer for the G5187 (UC0 serial, 32 MHz). Arduino's Blink, unchanged, and a new boardcheck sketch flashed and ran: the LED pin toggled at the expected half periods when read through the debug port, and boardcheck printed its banner and a millis and micros line each second at 115200.
rows.limits: Blink and a serial and GPIO check only; SPI and Wire were built and not run, and the display libraries are not built for this board. AnalogReadSerial does not compile (the layer has no analogRead).
rows.why: It shows the layer moves to a second MSPM0 part with a board folder and two small shared-code changes.

rows.number: ML-KEM-768 keygen 757,000 cycles (0.95 ms); ML-DSA-44 sign 4.16 million cycles (5.2 ms)
rows.title: Post-quantum known-answer tests pass and run on the LP-AM243's Cortex-R5F
rows.says: The shared post-quantum core (ML-KEM-768 and ML-DSA-44, default parameters) builds for the R5F with TI Arm Clang and passes NIST's known-answer tests on the board in 3 of 3 loads. At 800 MHz keygen takes 0.95 ms, encapsulation 1.08 ms, decapsulation 1.34 ms; ML-DSA-44 keygen 2.4 ms, sign 5.2 ms, verify 2.5 ms.
rows.limits: Run from RAM with caches on and a fixed-seed random generator (timing does not depend on it); one board; the key exchange with a Mac was not run.
rows.why: It puts a fourth core family next to the Cortex-M0+, M33 and C28x numbers.

rows.number: 19 of 19 REPL checks pass; (tak 18 12 6) in 8.1 s
rows.title: uLisp runs on the LAUNCHXL-F2800137's C28x
rows.says: uLisp, written for 32-bit Arm chips, gives a Lisp prompt on the C2000 chip's serial port after three source changes for its 16-bit int and 16-bit char: 19 of 19 REPL checks pass in each of 3 runs, (tak 18 12 6) takes 8.1 to 8.2 s and (fib 23) 5.3 to 5.4 s at 120 MHz. The image goes in flash from a raw binary; the restore read back identical.
rows.limits: One board, run from flash. The LED level was read back through the GPIO driver, not seen, and the stack guard was not exercised. The C28x does the same work in 1.3 times less time than the CC2340R5 at 48 MHz but needs 2.5 times the clocks.
rows.why: A 16-bit-char core runs the same interpreter, with the cost of each fix recorded.

rows.number: Lisp REPL checks pass; (tak 18 12 6) in 0.91 s
rows.title: uLisp runs on the LP-AM243's Cortex-R5F
rows.says: A new board layer (console on UART0, a timer from the SDK, the board LED) runs uLisp: all 20 REPL checks pass in 3 of 3 loads, (fib 23) takes 0.70 s and (tak 18 12 6) 0.91 s at 800 MHz.
rows.limits: RAM load, one board; the LED level was read back from the GPIO register, not seen; the time is 2.5 times slower than the CC2755P10 figure scaled by clock, cause not found.
rows.why: Another core family for the same interpreter.

rows.number: Four room-occupancy models, 20 of 20 vectors; 0.12 ms to 5.1 ms at -O3
rows.title: The four occupancy models run in plain C on the LP-AM243's Cortex-R5F
rows.says: Every answer matched on all 20 stored windows in all builds and loads; fastest vector, -O3 at 800 MHz: 95,661 cycles (0.12 ms) for the 636-weight model, 260,800 (0.33 ms), 1,094,832 (1.37 ms), and 4,072,488 (5.09 ms) for the 32,836-weight model.
rows.limits: One board, plain C only; no accelerator on this chip family was used.
rows.why: It adds a fast real-time core to the same timing table.

rows.title: TI's FreeRTOS task-switch example runs on the LP-AM243's Cortex-R5F
rows.says: The SDK's task_switch example, built with the SDK makefile and loaded to RAM, timed 2,000,000 switches per case: 2.44 us with a semaphore, 1.96 us with a notification and 2.70 us task to ISR to task, identical in 3 loads.
rows.limits: TI's page lists 0.76 us for the semaphore case; ours is about 3 times slower, not explained. A taskYIELD round-trip harness was not written.
rows.why: It gives the R5F a task-switch row in the common table.

rows.number: 8.4 s from build to flashed blink
rows.title: TI's blink builds and flashes on the LP-MSPM0L2228 from a Mac terminal, first day
rows.says: TI's gpio_toggle_output builds in 2.5 to 3.6 s and flashes with DSLite in 4.2 to 4.8 s; the GPIO output registers change between reads. CoreMark at 32 MHz scores 74.58 per second at -O3.
rows.limits: Blink period not timed (one DSLite read takes about 2 s); the LCD glass was not seen; OpenOCD flashing and tools/frl not run.
rows.why: A new LaunchPad with an LCD builds and flashes the same way as the others.

rows.title: A 32 MHz MSPM0L2228 runs four room-occupancy models and two handwriting models
rows.says: The four room-occupancy models (636 to 32,836 weights) run as plain C at -O3 in 9.4, 21.4, 81.6 and 294.5 ms, every one right on all 20 test vectors. BitNetMCU's 1k and 12k models read 10 of 10 digits in 94,251 and 443,117 cycles. TI's UART example prints a changed message at 115200.
rows.limits: Plain C only; TI's NNC build and the larger BitNetMCU models were not run on this board. Latency is the fastest of 20 vectors at one clock.
rows.why: A 32 MHz Cortex-M0+ with a segment LCD runs the same edge AI models as the bigger MSPM0 boards.
